title: One-way functions from P ≠ NP
subfield: Foundations and minimal assumptions
open: Does the assumption P ≠ NP by itself suffice to guarantee that one-way functions exist? More precisely, is there a construction or reduction showing that worst-case hardness in NP yields cryptographic (average-case) hardness?
status: Open for decades. Worst-case-to-average-case reductions face substantial barriers, and worst-case hardness is not presently interchangeable with cryptographic average-case hardness. Key work: Akavia, Goldreich, Goldwasser, and Moshkovitz, 2005, *On Basing One-Way Functions on NP-Hardness*.
solved_when: A proof that one-way functions exist under the sole assumption P ≠ NP, or a proof that this implication fails (e.g., a relativized or oracle world where P ≠ NP yet one-way functions do not exist).
why: It would tie the central conjecture of complexity theory directly to the foundations of cryptographic security, establishing the weakest possible assumption for cryptography — or reveal that cryptography requires strictly stronger assumptions.
key_works: Akavia, Goldreich, Goldwasser, and Moshkovitz, 2005, *On Basing One-Way Functions on NP-Hardness*.

title: Collision-resistant hashing from arbitrary one-way functions
subfield: Foundations and minimal assumptions
open: Can collision-resistant hash families be built from arbitrary one-way functions? More precisely, is there a construction that circumvents the known black-box separations between one-way functions and collision resistance?
status: A longstanding open problem. Simon (1998, *Finding Collisions on a One-Way Street: Can Secure Hash Functions Be Based on General Assumptions?*) established separations distinguishing collision resistance from the hashing properties routinely obtained from one-way functions, and Couteau, Farshim, and Mahmoody (2021, *Black-Box Uselessness: Composing Separations in Cryptography*, ePrint 2021/016) extended the black-box separation framework.
solved_when: A construction of collision-resistant hash families from arbitrary one-way functions is given, in a manner not excluded by black-box lower bounds (or, alternatively, a proof that no such construction exists).
why: Collision resistance underpins commitments, authenticated data structures, and many proof systems, so resolving this determines whether those primitives rest on the minimal assumption in cryptography.
key_works: Simon, 1998, *Finding Collisions on a One-Way Street: Can Secure Hash Functions Be Based on General Assumptions?*; Couteau, Farshim, and Mahmoody, 2021, *Black-Box Uselessness: Composing Separations in Cryptography*, ePrint 2021/016.

title: Injective one-way functions from general one-way functions
subfield: Foundations and minimal assumptions
open: Can every one-way function be transformed into an injective one-way function, using no assumption beyond the original function's own hardness? Formally, is there a black-box-style construction of injective one-way functions from arbitrary (possibly many-to-one) one-way functions?
status: Open. Injective one-way functions are known to follow from particular number-theoretic assumptions, but no general transformation from arbitrary one-way functions is known (Goldreich, Levin, and Nisan, 1995, *On Constructing 1-1 One-Way Functions*, ECCC TR95-029).
solved_when: A construction is given that starts from any one-way function and produces an injective one-way function, assuming no additional hardness beyond the given one-way function.
why: Injectivity simplifies commitments, authentication, and cryptographic reductions, so a general transformation would make these primitives available under the minimal assumption in cryptography.
key_works: Goldreich, Levin, and Nisan, 1995, *On Constructing 1-1 One-Way Functions*, ECCC TR95-029.

title: One-way permutations from one-way functions
subfield: Foundations and minimal assumptions
open: Do arbitrary one-way functions imply the existence of efficiently evaluable, length-preserving one-way permutations? Put formally, is permutation structure a free consequence of the one-way function assumption, or a genuinely stronger one?
status: A longstanding open problem. Care is needed with definitions: variants involving keyed families and restricted domains do not automatically settle the question of permutations defined on all bit strings (Goldreich, 2005, *On One-Way Permutations: A Clarification*; Goldreich, Levin, and Nisan, 1995, *On Constructing 1-1 One-Way Functions*).
solved_when: A proof that every one-way function yields an efficiently evaluable, length-preserving one-way permutation, or a proof (e.g., via a black-box or relativized separation) that it does not.
why: A positive answer would make permutation-based cryptographic constructions available under the minimal one-way function assumption; a negative answer would establish permutation structure as an additional assumption that must be assumed separately.
key_works: Goldreich, 2005, *On One-Way Permutations: A Clarification*; Goldreich, Levin, and Nisan, 1995, *On Constructing 1-1 One-Way Functions*.

title: Goldreich-generator security against unrestricted efficient distinguishers
subfield: Foundations and minimal assumptions
open: Can Goldreich's pseudorandom generator, with a suitable polynomial stretch, be proved pseudorandom against all polynomial-time distinguishers, starting from an assumption that is clearly stated and independently motivated?
status: Since Goldreich's local-function proposal, concrete attacks and restricted-model analyses have constrained the admissible predicates and stretch, but none of this establishes security against unrestricted efficient distinguishers (Couteau, Dupin, Méaux, Rossi, and Rotella, 2018, *On the Concrete Security of Goldreich's Pseudorandom Generator*, ePrint 2018/1162).
solved_when: A proof establishes that a Goldreich local generator with suitable polynomial stretch fools every polynomial-time distinguisher, under a stated assumption that is independently motivated beyond the generator itself.
why: Local pseudorandomness would enable exceptionally cheap cryptographic computation.
key_works: Couteau, Dupin, Méaux, Rossi, and Rotella, 2018, *On the Concrete Security of Goldreich’s Pseudorandom Generator*, ePrint 2018/1162.

title: Classical polynomial-time integer factorization
subfield: Classical public-key cryptanalysis and computational number theory
open: Does there exist a classical randomized algorithm that factors arbitrary integers in polynomial time? Equivalently, either exhibit such an algorithm or prove meaningful lower bounds for factoring in a sufficiently expressive computational model.
status: The problem has been open for decades; quantum polynomial-time algorithms exist but do not resolve the classical question. Related directions include BPP versus BQP and arithmetic circuit complexity (see Boneh and Shoup, 2023, *A Graduate Course in Applied Cryptography*; Galbraith, 2012, *Mathematics of Public Key Cryptography*).
solved_when: A classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm for factoring arbitrary integers is given, or a meaningful lower bound is established in a sufficiently expressive computational model.
why: A solution would transform computational number theory and invalidate factoring-based cryptography.
key_works: Boneh and Shoup, 2023, *A Graduate Course in Applied Cryptography*; Galbraith, 2012, *Mathematics of Public Key Cryptography*.

title: RSA inversion versus factoring
subfield: Classical public-key cryptanalysis and computational number theory
open: Does an efficient algorithm for inverting RSA on random messages necessarily yield an efficient algorithm for factoring the RSA modulus? The question is unrestricted: the equivalence must hold for arbitrary adversaries, not only those confined to a generic algebraic model.
status: Open since RSA's introduction. Generic-ring equivalence results — notably Aggarwal and Maurer, 2009, *Breaking RSA Generically Is Equivalent to Factoring* — establish the equivalence only in the generic model and do not settle the unrestricted case.
solved_when: A proof (or refutation) that inverting RSA and factoring are equivalent in the unrestricted computational setting, with no generic-model restriction on the reduction.
why: It determines whether RSA's security genuinely rests on the hardness of factoring or on a potentially weaker assumption.
key_works: Aggarwal and Maurer, 2009, *Breaking RSA Generically Is Equivalent to Factoring*.

title: Computational Diffie–Hellman versus discrete logarithms
subfield: Classical public-key cryptanalysis and computational number theory
open: When does the ability to solve the computational Diffie–Hellman problem in a group actually let you compute discrete logarithms? The goal is to establish general conditions — ideally covering cryptographically relevant prime-order groups without auxiliary smoothness assumptions — under which a CDH solver yields an efficient discrete-logarithm algorithm.
status: Open in general. Reductions from CDH to discrete logarithms are known only under additional group-order and number-theoretic conditions, notably in Maurer (1994, *Towards the Equivalence of Breaking the Diffie-Hellman Protocol and Computing Discrete Logarithms*, DOI 10.1007/3-540-48658-5_26). Related lines of inquiry include smooth numbers in short intervals and finite-field algorithms.
solved_when: A reduction is proved that, given an efficient CDH oracle, computes discrete logarithms efficiently in general prime-order groups, without relying on smoothness or additional group-order and number-theoretic conditions.
why: It would pin down the exact assumption underlying Diffie–Hellman protocols, telling cryptographers whether CDH hardness is genuinely independent of discrete-log hardness or merely an artifact of missing reductions.
key_works: Maurer, 1994, *Towards the Equivalence of Breaking the Diffie-Hellman Protocol and Computing Discrete Logarithms*, DOI 10.1007/3-540-48658-5_26.

title: Non-generic attacks on ordinary prime-order elliptic curves
subfield: Classical public-key cryptanalysis and computational number theory
open: Is there a classical algorithm that computes discrete logarithms on ordinary, prime-order elliptic curves faster than the generic square-root bound? Formally, find an asymptotically sub-square-root classical discrete-logarithm algorithm that does not rely on an already excluded special structure of the curve.
status: Open. Generic-group lower bounds do not exclude algorithms using the explicit curve representation. Reference: Galbraith, 2012, *Mathematics of Public Key Cryptography*, elliptic-curve discrete logarithms.
solved_when: An explicit classical algorithm, together with an asymptotic running-time analysis, breaks the square-root barrier (i.e., runs in time $o(\sqrt{n})$ where $n$ is the group order) on ordinary prime-order elliptic curves lacking the excluded special structures.
why: It is a central unresolved security question for elliptic-curve cryptography: a positive answer would undermine the concrete security estimates underlying widely deployed elliptic-curve systems.
key_works: Galbraith, 2012, *Mathematics of Public Key Cryptography*, elliptic-curve discrete logarithms.

title: Rigorous multivariate Coppersmith criteria
subfield: Classical public-key cryptanalysis and computational number theory
open: When can we rigorously guarantee that Coppersmith-type lattice methods find all small integer roots of a multivariate polynomial? Formally, give efficiently checkable conditions under which lattice-generated multivariate polynomial relations provably yield every intended small root, without heuristic algebraic-independence assumptions.
status: The problem has stood since the 1990s. Successful cryptanalytic applications coexist with a persistent gap between lattice reduction and guaranteed root extraction, so the gap remains open.
solved_when: A set of efficiently checkable conditions is given and proved under which the lattice-based construction recovers all small roots of the multivariate polynomials, with no algebraic-independence heuristic required.
why: It would separate proved cryptanalytic attacks — e.g., against RSA as in Coppersmith's and Boneh–Durfee's settings — from methods that merely work experimentally, closing a foundational gap in the security arguments that depend on them.
key_works: Coppersmith, 1997, *Small Solutions to Polynomial Equations, and Low Exponent RSA Vulnerabilities*; Boneh–Durfee, 1999, *Cryptanalysis of RSA with Private Key \(d\) Less than \(N^{0.292}\)*.

title: Optimal RSA reconstruction thresholds from random leaked bits
subfield: Classical public-key cryptanalysis and computational number theory
open: When an attacker obtains randomly positioned bits of specified RSA secret components, how many bits suffice to reconstruct the full private key in polynomial time? The goal is sharp thresholds, cleanly separating information-theoretic identifiability from efficient algorithmic recovery.
status: The problem has been active since the 2000s. Heninger and Shacham (2009, *Reconstructing RSA Private Keys from Random Key Bits*, ePrint 2008/510) showed reconstruction exploiting redundancy across RSA key components; the required thresholds depend strongly on which components leak.
solved_when: For each leakage pattern (i.e., each subset of RSA key components whose bits are revealed), a polynomial-time reconstruction algorithm is given with matching lower bounds establishing that fewer revealed bits cannot yield unique identification.
why: It would precisely quantify the damage caused by partial memory disclosure, telling practitioners exactly how many leaked bits make an RSA key recoverable.
key_works: Heninger and Shacham, 2009, *Reconstructing RSA Private Keys from Random Key Bits*, ePrint 2008/510.

title: The \(d<N^{1/2}\) small-private-exponent RSA target
subfield: Classical public-key cryptanalysis and computational number theory
open: Can every balanced RSA modulus whose private exponent satisfies \(d<N^{1/2-\varepsilon}\) be broken efficiently, under appropriate standard parameter conditions?

solved_when: An efficient attack (or a proof of security under standard assumptions) is given covering all \(d<N^{1/2-\varepsilon}\), closing the gap between the known \(N^{0.292}\) bound and the \(N^{1/2}\) threshold.
why: It would settle a prominent boundary in RSA cryptanalysis, determining exactly how small a private exponent can be before the system becomes unsafe.

title: Fröberg’s conjecture for generic forms
subfield: Code-based, multivariate, and isogeny-based cryptography
open: Does the ideal generated by a collection of generic homogeneous forms always have the Hilbert series predicted by Fröberg? A proof is still missing in the general parameter regimes, beyond the many degrees, variable counts, and special cases already settled.
status: Open since 1985. Numerous degrees, variable counts, and special cases are settled, but the general conjecture remains unproved; partial results include Nenashev, 2017, *A Note on Fröberg's Conjecture for Forms of Equal Degrees*, DOI 10.1016/j.crma.2017.01.011, and Trung, arXiv:1803.04997.
solved_when: The conjectured Hilbert series is established for generic homogeneous forms in all previously unresolved general parameter regimes.
why: The predicted Hilbert series underpins the algebraic regularity assumptions used to estimate the complexity of solving polynomial systems, so settling it places those complexity estimates on firm algebraic ground.
key_works: Nenashev, 2017, *A Note on Fröberg’s Conjecture for Forms of Equal Degrees*, DOI 10.1016/j.crma.2017.01.011; Trung, arXiv:1803.04997.

title: Proving semi-regularity assumptions for random Boolean systems
subfield: Code-based, multivariate, and isogeny-based cryptography
open: Can we prove that a random quadratic system over \(\mathbb F_2\) is, with high probability, algebraically regular in the sharp sense the heuristics assume — so that cryptanalytic solving-time estimates for such systems rest on theorems rather than experiments?
status: Algorithms with strong conditional bounds and supporting experiments exist (Bardet, Faugère, Salvy, and Spaenlehauer, 2013, *On the Complexity of Solving Quadratic Boolean Systems*, arXiv:1112.6263; DOI 10.1016/j.jco.2012.07.001), but these are not unconditional typical-case analyses.
solved_when: An unconditional high-probability regularity statement is proved for random quadratic Boolean systems that matches the semi-regular (Bardet–Faugère–Salvy–Spaenlehauer-style) degree bounds closely enough to justify the conditional solving-time estimates used in multivariate security analyses.
why: It would turn multivariate cryptographic security estimates from heuristic, experimentally supported extrapolations into mathematically firm typical-case complexity bounds.
key_works: Bardet, Faugère, Salvy, and Spaenlehauer, 2013, *On the Complexity of Solving Quadratic Boolean Systems*, arXiv:1112.6263; DOI 10.1016/j.jco.2012.07.001.

title: Fully audited constant-time SQIsign signing
subfield: Code-based, multivariate, and isogeny-based cryptography
open: Can the SQIsign scheme be implemented end-to-end so that every secret-dependent computation — arithmetic, sampling, memory access, and exceptional control-flow paths — provably conforms to a verified leakage model?
status: Constant-time four-dimensional lattice-reduction work (Hanyecz et al., 2025, *Constant Time Lattice Reduction in Dimension 4 with Application to SQIsign*) addresses an important subroutine of the signing process, but does not automatically yield a constant-time implementation of the entire scheme. solved_when: A complete, audited SQIsign signing implementation exists in which all secret-dependent arithmetic, sampling, memory behavior, and exceptional paths satisfy a verified leakage model.
why: Compact post-quantum signatures are of little use if the act of signing leaks the private key through side channels.

title: An eight-bit APN permutation
subfield: Boolean functions, S-boxes, and finite geometry
open: Does there exist an almost-perfect-nonlinear (APN) permutation on the vector space \(\mathbb F_2^8\)? Formally: find such a permutation, or prove that none can exist.
status: The known six-bit example does not extend the existence result to eight bits, and major families and structural approaches have been excluded; see Calderini, Sala, and Villa, 2017, *A Note on APN Permutations in Even Dimension*, DOI 10.1016/j.ffa.2017.02.001.

why: It would provide an optimal-differential permutation at the ubiquitous byte size, the dimension on which essentially all practical symmetric ciphers operate.

title: APN permutations in infinitely many even dimensions
subfield: Boolean functions, S-boxes, and finite geometry
open: Does there exist an infinite family of APN permutations in an even number of variables greater than six, or is there an obstruction that forbids such families entirely?
status: Open. Generalized Kim-type constructions have yielded substantial negative results rather than a general solution; Chase and Lisonek (2020, *Kim-Type APN Functions Are Affine Equivalent to Gold Functions*, arXiv:2009.05937) showed Kim-type APN functions are affine equivalent to Gold functions.
solved_when: Either an explicit infinite family of APN permutations is constructed in even dimensions n > 6, or a proof is given that no such family can exist.
why: It would settle whether the known six-bit phenomenon is exceptional among even dimensions.
key_works: Chase and Lisonek, 2020, *Kim-Type APN Functions Are Affine Equivalent to Gold Functions*, arXiv:2009.05937.

title: The exceptional APN conjecture
subfield: Boolean functions, S-boxes, and finite geometry
open: Which polynomial functions are almost perfect nonlinear (APN) on infinitely many extensions of their base finite field — and is it true that only the Gold and Kasami–Welch monomials, up to the relevant equivalence, have this property?
status: The general problem remains open; special degree families have been eliminated or classified. Recent special-case resolutions must not be mistaken for the full conjecture (Aubry et al., 2022–2023, *Polynomials with Maximal Differential Uniformity and the Exceptional APN Conjecture*, arXiv:2207.13945).
solved_when: Every polynomial that is APN over infinitely many extension fields is shown to be equivalent to a Gold or Kasami–Welch function, with no remaining exceptional cases.
why: It would give a complete classification of indefinitely extensible optimal differential constructions, determining once and for all which S-boxes can retain maximal resistance to differential attacks across arbitrary extension degrees.
key_works: Aubry et al., 2022–2023, *Polynomials with Maximal Differential Uniformity and the Exceptional APN Conjecture*, arXiv:2207.13945.

title: Maximum Boolean nonlinearity in odd dimensions
subfield: Boolean functions, S-boxes, and finite geometry
open: What is the largest possible nonlinearity of a Boolean function in each odd number of variables for which it remains unknown, and how does this maximum grow asymptotically? Equivalently, what is the covering radius of the first-order Reed–Muller code \(RM(1,n)\) for unresolved odd \(n\)?
status: A longstanding open problem. solved_when: The exact covering radius of \(RM(1,n)\) is determined for every odd \(n\) (or at least for an infinite family beyond the known cases), together with the asymptotic behavior of the maximum nonlinearity as the number of variables grows.
why: The nonlinearity of a Boolean function measures its resistance to affine approximation attacks; knowing the maximum pins down the best achievable security bound for S-boxes and stream-cipher filtering functions.

title: A substantial single-key attack on full AES-128
subfield: Symmetric cryptanalysis and hash functions
open: Does there exist a single-key key-recovery attack on full AES-128 that achieves a substantial advantage over exhaustive search, under explicitly bounded data and memory? The question is whether AES-128's security against classical single-key adversaries can be meaningfully undercut in practice, not merely in asymptotic terms.
status: The best-known result is biclique cryptanalysis, which provides only a slight theoretical improvement over exhaustive search and does not constitute a practical break (Bogdanov, Khovratovich, and Rechberger, 2011, *Biclique Cryptanalysis of the Full AES*, ePrint 2011/449).
solved_when: A full-round, single-key key-recovery attack on AES-128 is demonstrated whose advantage over exhaustive search is substantial (not a marginal theoretical gain), with the data and memory requirements of the attack explicitly bounded.
why: Such an attack would expose structure in AES-128 that current security assessments fail to capture, forcing a re-evaluation of the assumptions underlying its deployment.
key_works: Bogdanov, Khovratovich, and Rechberger, 2011, *Biclique Cryptanalysis of the Full AES*, ePrint 2011/449.

title: Full SHA-256 collisions below birthday complexity
subfield: Symmetric cryptanalysis and hash functions
open: Can collisions for the full, unmodified SHA-256 hash function be found with total work substantially below the generic birthday bound of \(2^{128}\) evaluations? In other words, does the standard function admit a shortcut collision attack, or does it behave like an ideal hash?
status: Existing results cover reduced-round variants or modified initial states; none of these solves the standard-function problem, and no attack on full SHA-256 below the birthday scale is known.
solved_when: A collision for full, untruncated SHA-256 (standard initial state, no structural modifications) is exhibited by an algorithm whose total work is substantially below \(2^{128}\).
why: Collision resistance of SHA-256 underpins digital signatures, commitments, and content addressing; a shortcut attack would force migration or re-engineering of these widely deployed primitives.
key_works: NIST, 2015, *Secure Hash Standard*, FIPS 180-4.

title: Full SHA-256 preimages below generic search
subfield: Symmetric cryptanalysis and hash functions
open: Can the full SHA-256 function be inverted on independently specified outputs substantially faster than the generic \(2^{256}\)-scale brute-force search? More precisely, is there a classical algorithm finding preimages of arbitrary SHA-256 digests at a cost meaningfully below the generic bound?
status: The problem remains open for the full function; reduced-round preimage results exist but do not settle it, and it is distinct from collision finding. The function is specified in NIST, 2015, *Secure Hash Standard*, FIPS 180-4.
solved_when: A classical algorithm produces preimages for independently specified SHA-256 outputs with a substantial asymptotic or concrete advantage over \(2^{256}\)-scale generic search; reduced-round results do not count.
why: It certifies the preimage-resistance property relied on by commitments and hash-based constructions, a security property distinct from collision resistance.

title: Full SHA3-256 preimages below generic search
subfield: Symmetric cryptanalysis and hash functions
open: Can we recover a preimage of a specified full SHA3-256 digest with a substantial classical advantage over generic search? In other words, is there an attack on the complete, unreduced SHA3-256 meaningfully faster than brute-force preimage search?
status: No such preimage attack is known; the problem is understood to be separate from collisions, distinguishers, and reduced-round attacks on the underlying permutation. title: Constant-time security under dynamic voltage and frequency scaling
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: Can we define and enforce a notion of constant-time security when a processor's frequency scaling makes execution time depend on secret-dependent power draw? status: Hertzbleed (Wang, Paccagnella, He, Shacham, and Fletcher, 2022, *Hertzbleed: Turning Power Side-Channel Attacks into Remote Timing Attacks on x86*) demonstrated that constant instruction timing is not sufficient against this mechanism. why: It breaks the central abstraction underlying software side-channel defense: that identical instruction sequences imply identical observable timing. Without a repair, every constant-time cryptographic implementation in deployment remains remotely attackable.

title: R11.07. The optimal resilience of two-round full-information coin flipping
subfield: Round 11
open: What is the largest adversarial coalition that a two-round full-information collective coin-flipping protocol, in which each participant broadcasts one bit per round, can tolerate? Equivalently, close the gap between the known achievable resilience and the known attacks for this model.

title: Transparent SNARK with constant proofs and linear-time proving

why: It would be the "everything SNARK": verification cheap enough for blockchains and browsers, no trust ceremony, and quantum-safe — removing the trade-off where today one must sacrifice either succinctness, prover efficiency, transparency, or post-quantum security.

title: Witness encryption for all of NP from standard assumptions

title: General two-party secret-key capacity
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: When two honest parties and an eavesdropper each observe correlated data drawn from an arbitrary finite joint distribution, how much secret key can the two parties reliably extract? The goal is an exact asymptotic expression for this two-party secret-key capacity in full generality.
status: Only general lower and upper bounds are known; the July 2026 existence result for bipartite bound information (Pauwels–Gisin–Renner, arXiv:2607.25838) does not supply a complete capacity formula. Key works: Maurer, 1993, DOI 10.1109/18.256484; Maurer–Wolf, 1999, *Intrinsic Conditional Information*; Pauwels–Gisin–Renner, 2026, arXiv:2607.25838.
solved_when: A formula for the secret-key capacity of an arbitrary finite triple of observations is established and shown tight, with matching achievability and converse for the general case.
why: It would characterize the secrecy inherently present in correlated data, giving a complete answer to what correlations are worth as a cryptographic resource.
key_works: Maurer, 1993, DOI 10.1109/18.256484; Maurer–Wolf, 1999, *Intrinsic Conditional Information*; Pauwels–Gisin–Renner, 2026, arXiv:2607.25838.

title: Deciding positive distillable secrecy
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Given a finite rational probability distribution shared by two parties, is there an effective general procedure to decide whether they can distill a positive amount of secret key from it through unrestricted public discussion?
status: The natural approach of identifying positive distillable key with positive secrecy-formation cost is blocked: bound information has been shown to exist (Pauwels, Gisin, and Renner, 2026, *Bipartite Bound Information Exists*, arXiv:2607.25838), so distributions can carry secrecy that cannot be distilled.
solved_when: An algorithm (or equivalent effective criterion) is provided that, for any finite rational distribution, decides in finitely many steps whether the two-party distillable secret key under public discussion is positive.
why: Such a criterion would cleanly separate correlations that are useful for key agreement from those that carry only nondistillable, bound secrecy.
key_works: Pauwels, Gisin, and Renner, 2026, *Bipartite Bound Information Exists*, arXiv:2607.25838.

title: Explicit two-split-state non-malleable codes approaching capacity
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Can we construct explicit, efficient information-theoretic non-malleable codes in the two-split-state model whose rate approaches the capacity of \(1/2\) with negligible error? That is, closing the gap between known explicit constructions and the information-theoretic capacity bound.
status: The capacity of \(1/2\) for this setting is known (Cheraghchi–Guruswami, 2013–2014, *Capacity of Non-Malleable Codes*, arXiv:1309.0458), and explicit rate-one-third constructions (Aggarwal et al., 2022, *Rate One-Third Non-malleable Codes*) are an important milestone; computational and extra-state results belong to different settings.
solved_when: An explicit two-split-state non-malleable code is given with rate tending to \(1/2\) and negligible error, with efficient encoding and decoding.
why: It would close a major explicit-construction gap in information-theoretic tamper resistance, matching the known capacity with practical codes.
key_works: Cheraghchi–Guruswami, 2013–2014, *Capacity of Non-Malleable Codes*, arXiv:1309.0458; Aggarwal et al., 2022, *Rate One-Third Non-malleable Codes*.

title: R11.09. Perfectly fair leader election beyond commit-and-reveal lower bounds
subfield: Round 11
open: Does the logarithmic-round barrier for perfect game-theoretic fairness in leader election reflect a fundamental limit, or only a limitation of commit-and-reveal-style protocols? Formally, is there a protocol outside that class that elects a leader with perfect fairness — each honest participant elected with probability at least \(1/n\) — against coalitions of size \(n^\varepsilon\), under the same abort and fairness definitions?
status: A TCC 2024 work by Ohad Klein, Ilan Komargodski, and Chenzhi Zhu (2024/2025, *On the (Im)possibility of Game-Theoretically Fair Leader Election Protocols*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-031-78011-0_13) proves an \(\Omega(\log n)\) lower bound for the restricted commit-and-reveal protocol class. Known sublogarithmic protocols achieve only approximate fairness under weaker coalition requirements, and so do not answer this question.
solved_when: A protocol (or impossibility proof) is exhibited for coalitions of size \(n^\varepsilon\) preserving election probability at least \(1/n\) for every honest participant, under the same abort and fairness definitions, and it either breaks the \(\Omega(\log n)\) round barrier outside the commit-and-reveal class or proves the barrier extends to all protocols.
why: It would distinguish a fundamental fairness barrier from an artifact of a familiar protocol architecture, determining whether perfect game-theoretic fairness is achievable in sublogarithmic rounds at all.
key_works: Ohad Klein, Ilan Komargodski, and Chenzhi Zhu, 2024/2025, *On the (Im)possibility of Game-Theoretically Fair Leader Election Protocols*, DOI:10.1007/978-3-031-78011-0_13.

title: R11.11. A rigorous constant-space family for finite-penalty quantum coin flipping
subfield: Round 11
open: For a fixed finite cheating penalty, can one prove a constant-qubit family of quantum coin-flipping protocols whose maximum dishonest expected payoff tends to \(1/2\) as the family grows? A concrete target is 24 qubits at penalty \(\Lambda=0.01\).

solved_when: A rigorously proved protocol family exists with constant qubit cost — ideally the concrete target of 24 qubits with penalty \(\Lambda=0.01\) — whose maximum dishonest expected payoff approaches \(1/2\) for arbitrarily small bias \(\varepsilon>0\).
why: It would convert numerical point-game evidence into an asymptotic resource theorem, establishing constant space as sufficient for near-fair finite-penalty coin flipping.
key_works: Arora, Miller, Morales, and Sikora, 2025, *Cheat-Penalised Quantum Weak Coin-Flipping*, arXiv:2510.03218.

title: R11.19. Bit-polynomial-time decoding behind the new capacity theorem
subfield: Round 11
open: For a Reed–Solomon code at any fixed slack from capacity, can the new capacity-achieving list decoder be made to run in time polynomial in the block length \(n\) and the bit length \(\log q\), while preserving its decoding radius and complete output list?

why: It would separate an algorithmic existence theorem from genuine scalability over cryptographic-size fields, where bit length rather than field cardinality is the right cost measure.

title: Verifiable computation on encrypted data (FHE × ZK)
subfield: Trust-minimization systems (MPC + ZK + FHE combinations)
open: Can a cloud server prove, in zero knowledge, that it correctly evaluated a computation on encrypted data it cannot decrypt — so that the proof reveals nothing beyond the correctness of the output? Formally, this asks for a combined FHE-plus-ZK scheme achieving verifiable FHE where the added proof overhead stays within 10x of plain FHE evaluation.
status: The Gentry–Wichs impossibility result (STOC 2011) separates proof-of-correctness from information-theoretic checking, ruling out the strongest forms of verification. Succinct ZK proofs over homomorphic ciphertexts exist but only at significant overhead; current VC-over-FHE approaches such as PINNs and GIPs add substantial cost. The practical combined runtime meeting the 10x target remains open. Key works: Gennaro–Gentry–Parno verifiable computation (2010); Gentry–Wichs (STOC 2011); FHE+SNARK hybrid lines (verify).
solved_when: A construction exists in which a server homomorphically evaluates a circuit on FHE ciphertexts and produces a zero-knowledge, succinct proof of correct evaluation, with the combined overhead (proof generation and verification, relative to plain FHE evaluation of the same circuit) at most 10x.
why: It completes the full stack of delegated encrypted computation — confidentiality from FHE, integrity from ZK, and succinctness — realizing the "don't trust the cloud at all" guarantee.
key_works: Gennaro–Gentry–Parno verifiable computation (2010); Gentry–Wichs (STOC 2011); FHE+SNARK hybrid lines (verify).

why: A positive answer would bridge private-key and public-key cryptography, showing public-key primitives need no more than the minimal assumption underlying symmetric cryptography.

solved_when: A fabricated accelerator has reproducibly measured energy and latency for complete application executions, with host work, transfers, memory, and key loading all included in the reported numbers.
why: It reveals whether accelerator gains survive deployment overhead; without it, kernel-level and projected figures cannot be trusted as predictors of real deployments.
key_works: Geelen et al., 2022, *BASALISC*, arXiv:2205.14017; Jiang, Lou, and Joshi, 2022, *MATCHA*, arXiv:2202.08814.

title: Compact bootstrapping keys without displaced costs
subfield: Fully homomorphic encryption
open: Can a fully homomorphic encryption scheme store its bootstrapping keys an order of magnitude more compactly than a pinned current implementation, without trading away security or shifting the savings into evaluation cost? Formally, achieve a tenfold reduction in bootstrapping-key storage while keeping the total homomorphic evaluation cost low enough that the net benefit survives.
status: This is currently a proposed joint optimization target; no solution is known. Existing approaches — compression, decomposition, and recomputation — trade storage against other resources, which is precisely the displaced-cost problem the target seeks to overcome.
solved_when: Bootstrapping-key storage is reduced tenfold relative to the pinned current implementation, with no loss of security and no increase in total evaluation cost large enough to erase the storage benefit.
why: Key material can dominate memory and determine whether deployment is feasible at all, so a genuine tenfold reduction would unlock FHE in memory-constrained settings rather than merely relocating the bottleneck.
key_works: Chillotti et al., *TFHE*, ePrint 2018/421; Bossuat et al., 2024–2025, *Security Guidelines for Implementing Homomorphic Encryption*, ePrint 2024/463.

title: Efficient circuit privacy for approximate homomorphic encryption
subfield: Fully homomorphic encryption
open: Can we construct an approximate homomorphic encryption scheme that hides the evaluated circuit and the intermediate numerical behavior of the computation, while still delivering useful accuracy and keeping noise growth manageable?
status: Approximate, circuit-private, and multiparty notions require careful distinctions, and newer constructions — such as Kluczniak and Santato, 2025, *On Circuit Private, Multikey and Threshold Approximate Homomorphic Encryption* — do not eliminate every efficiency tradeoff; the problem remains open per the CKKS research discussion of 2026.
solved_when: A construction achieves circuit privacy for approximate homomorphic encryption with both accuracy preserved to a useful level and noise growth that does not render the scheme impractical, without sacrificing the efficiency tradeoffs left open by current constructions.
why: Data privacy alone does not protect proprietary models or private computations; without circuit privacy, whoever holds the evaluation keys or decryption results can learn information about the algorithm applied.
key_works: Kluczniak and Santato, 2025, *On Circuit Private, Multikey and Threshold Approximate Homomorphic Encryption*; CKKS research discussion, 2026.

title: Optimal protection against adaptive approximate-output leakage
subfield: Fully homomorphic encryption
open: What is the least amount of noise or protocol restriction that suffices to protect an approximate-output encryption scheme when an adversary can adaptively query and observe approximate decryptions? More formally, characterize the minimal perturbation of decrypted values (or constraints on decryption queries) needed to achieve a sound security notion under adaptive approximate-output leakage.
status: Li and Micciancio (2021, *On the Security of Homomorphic Encryption on Approximate Numbers*, ePrint 2020/1533; DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-77870-5_23) demonstrated that exposed approximation errors can undermine naïve security interpretations; this is not a ciphertext-only break of CKKS.
solved_when: A precise characterization exists of the minimum perturbation or protocol restrictions that provably secure schemes against adversaries who adaptively observe approximate decrypted outputs, together with matching attacks showing no weaker measure suffices.
why: Real applications of homomorphic encryption return numerical answers, not merely ciphertexts, so security must hold exactly in that approximate-output setting rather than under ciphertext-only assumptions.
key_works: Li and Micciancio, 2021, *On the Security of Homomorphic Encryption on Approximate Numbers*, ePrint 2020/1533; DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-77870-5_23.

title: Robust malicious multiparty approximate decryption
subfield: Fully homomorphic encryption
open: Can a set of parties jointly decrypt an approximate homomorphic ciphertext so that none of them — even acting maliciously — can turn the protocol into a decryption oracle or corrupt the decrypted value, while the scheme still tolerates malformed shares, adaptive decryption requests, and participant dropout at useful accuracy and throughput?
status: The relevant security and operational primitives exist in the literature; the open target is a construction that simultaneously meets their combined requirements for malicious-secure threshold approximate decryption. Key works include Kluczniak–Santato, 2025, *On Circuit Private, Multikey and Threshold Approximate Homomorphic Encryption*, and Li–Micciancio, 2021.
solved_when: A threshold approximate decryption protocol is specified that remains secure against malicious participants submitting malformed shares, adaptively chosen decryption requests, and dropout, while preserving decryption accuracy and throughput at practical levels for fully homomorphic encryption workloads.
why: Distributed key ownership should not silently introduce a decryption oracle or undetected numerical corruption into an otherwise secure FHE deployment.
key_works: Kluczniak–Santato, 2025, *On Circuit Private, Multikey and Threshold Approximate Homomorphic Encryption*; Li–Micciancio, 2021.

title: End-to-end verified numerical error in FHE compilers
subfield: Fully homomorphic encryption
open: Can we build a fully homomorphic encryption compiler that carries a machine-checkable certificate that every encrypted computation returns the correct answer, end to end — tracing numerical error from source-level semantics through approximation, quantization, rescaling, bootstrapping, and final decryption, even for adversarially chosen valid inputs?
status: Currently a proposed verification target. Existing cryptographic parameter guidance (Bossuat et al., 2024–2025, *Security Guidelines for Implementing Homomorphic Encryption*, ePrint 2024/463) does not prove numerical correctness. Related techniques include verified numerics and abstract interpretation.
solved_when: A verification framework exists that, for a compiled FHE program, proves a bound on application-level numerical error covering the full pipeline from source semantics to decryption, holds for all valid inputs including adversarially chosen ones, and is checked mechanically rather than derived from cryptographic parameter guidance.
why: Without end-to-end certification, a pipeline can silently return an encrypted wrong answer — and an encrypted wrong answer remains wrong; parameter choices that guarantee security give no guarantee of numerical correctness.
key_works: Bossuat et al., 2024–2025, *Security Guidelines for Implementing Homomorphic Encryption*, ePrint 2024/463.

title: Efficient persistent encrypted RAM computation
subfield: Fully homomorphic encryption
open: Can we build an encrypted RAM that supports long-running computation over dynamically updated memory with hidden access patterns, crash recovery, and substantially sublinear per-access overhead in realistic workloads?
status: FHE, PIR, and ORAM each supply relevant components, but their persistent, verified integration remains a distinct systems target.
solved_when: A persistent encrypted RAM system exists that hides access patterns, survives crashes, and achieves substantially sublinear per-access overhead under realistic workloads over long-running, mutable memory.
why: Real programs rely on mutable memory rather than fixed arithmetic circuits alone, so FHE computation on real software stalls without such a substrate.
key_works: Larsen–Nielsen, 2018, *Yes, There Is an Oblivious RAM Lower Bound!*, ePrint 2018/423; Li et al., 2023–2024, *Hintless Single-Server Private Information Retrieval*.

title: Explicit access structures requiring very large nonlinear shares
subfield: Secret sharing, secure computation, and correlated randomness
open: Can we write down a single, concretely described access structure and prove that every perfect secret-sharing scheme for it — linear or not — requires very large shares? A second sentence: give an explicit family of access structures, efficiently describable, with strong lower bounds against unrestricted perfect secret sharing.
status: Current knowledge consists of counting-style worst-case results and linear lower bounds; neither yields an explicit structure with a proven lower bound against unrestricted perfect secret sharing. The worst-case complexity of linear secret sharing was resolved by Nir, 2026, *Resolving the Worst-Case Complexity of Linear Secret Sharing*, ECCC TR26-146. Related lines of attack include explicit monotone circuit lower bounds and non-Shannon information inequalities.
solved_when: An explicitly constructed access structure (or efficiently describable family) is exhibited together with a proof of a strong share-size lower bound against all perfect secret-sharing schemes, linear and nonlinear alike.
why: Such an explicit construction would identify which real-world policy structures are intrinsically expensive to share secrets under, rather than relying on counting arguments that only show some hard structures exist.

title: Optimal arithmetic–Boolean conversion in malicious MPC
subfield: Secret sharing, secure computation, and correlated randomness
open: What is the true communication and preprocessing cost of converting between arithmetic and Boolean representations — including comparisons, truncation, and bit decomposition — in MPC with malicious adversaries, across different rings and adversary thresholds?
status: edaBits (Escudero, Ghosh, Keller, Rachuri, and Scholl, 2020, *Improved Primitives for MPC over Mixed Arithmetic-Binary Circuits*, ePrint 2020/338) deliver major improvements for arithmetic–Boolean conversion, but do not establish optimality over all parameter regimes.

why: These conversions often dominate mixed numerical and logical workloads, so optimal protocols directly reduce the cost of realistic secure computation.

title: Crash-safe, non-reusable MPC preprocessing
subfield: Secret sharing, secure computation, and correlated randomness
open: Can we build a distributed preprocessing lifecycle for MPC that guarantees correlations such as triples are never consumed twice, even across crashes, rollback, concurrent consumers, and partial commits? Formally, the goal is an infrastructure layer with provable exactly-once consumption of correlated randomness, sitting on top of (not altering) the algebraic correctness of the correlations themselves.
status: This is a proposed infrastructure target that goes beyond the algebraic correctness of triples or correlated bits; no construction is known. Related areas include exactly-once resource consumption and distributed transaction recovery. Key works: Keller, 2020, *MP-SPDZ*; Escudero et al., 2020, *Improved Primitives for MPC over Mixed Arithmetic-Binary Circuits*.
solved_when: A construction exists that provably never reuses correlations after crashes, rollback, concurrent consumers, or partial commit — i.e., a distributed preprocessing lifecycle with exactly-once resource consumption and recovery semantics.
why: A single reuse of one-time correlations can destroy the security of the entire computation; without crash-safe consumption, MPC preprocessing cannot be deployed reliably on real distributed infrastructure.
key_works: Keller, 2020, *MP-SPDZ*; Escudero et al., 2020, *Improved Primitives for MPC over Mixed Arithmetic-Binary Circuits*.

title: MPC under long-lived membership churn and mobile compromise
subfield: Secret sharing, secure computation, and correlated randomness
open: Can a multiparty computation service keep a formally specified corruption threshold intact while its participants are continuously replaced, refreshed, taken offline, and recovered — so that compromised shares never silently accumulate across epochs? In other words, can proactive and adaptive security techniques be carried through into a complete, operational implementation that survives long-lived membership churn and mobile compromise?
status: Proactive and adaptive techniques exist; a complete operational implementation is the proposed target. Related context includes Keller, 2020, *MP-SPDZ*; NIST, 2026, *Multi-Party Threshold Cryptography* project and call; mobile Byzantine faults; and reconfigurable distributed systems.
solved_when: A complete operational implementation exists that maintains the specified corruption threshold across participant replacement, refresh, downtime, and recovery, with no accumulation of compromised shares across epochs.
why: Real multiparty services outlive individual machines and administrators; without such a system, security guarantees erode silently as the fleet changes over time.
key_works: Keller, 2020, *MP-SPDZ*; NIST, 2026, *Multi-Party Threshold Cryptography* project and call.

why: It would place locally generated MPC correlations on standard-model foundations, removing the gap between the efficiency actually achieved in practice and what current proofs justify.

subfield: Secret sharing, secure computation, and correlated randomness

why: It would combine DCR-grade flexible correlations with post-quantum foundations, which DCR itself cannot offer.

subfield: Secret sharing, secure computation, and correlated randomness
open: Can a correlation-function setup protocol be turned into a durable multiparty service that survives failures and adversarial participants? Formally, this means extending setup with explicit honest-majority assumptions, checks on malicious inputs, restart safety, and unambiguous epoch changes.
status: A two-round distributed setup exists for important 2026 pseudorandom correlation functions, per Dutta et al., 2026, *New Pseudorandom Correlation Functions and Exponent VRFs from DCR*, ePrint 2026/2030; full service recovery remains a separate proposed target.
solved_when: A durable multiparty correlation-setup service is specified and realized with explicit honest-majority assumptions, malicious-input checks, restart safety after failures, and unambiguous epoch transitions.
why: Setup failures must not create correlated-key reuse or undetected bias in the resulting correlations.

title: Fairness classification beyond symmetric Boolean outputs
subfield: Secret sharing, secure computation, and correlated randomness
open: Which two-party functionalities with general finite or asymmetric outputs can be computed with complete fairness, beyond the symmetric Boolean case that is already understood? A full answer would give a characterization of the fair functionalities in this broader class, together with efficient protocols for each positive case.
status: Symmetric Boolean-output functions, including randomized ones, have a complete characterization (Asharov, Beimel, Makriyannis, and Omri, 2024, *Complete Characterization of Fairness in Secure Two-Party Computation of Boolean Functions*, DOI 10.1137/18M1232656); that solved case must be excluded, and nothing beyond it is settled.
solved_when: Every two-party functionality with general finite or asymmetric outputs is classified as either admitting complete fairness (with an efficient protocol) or provably not, and the symmetric Boolean case — including randomized functions, already characterized — is excluded.
why: It identifies when abort-based insecurity is fundamental rather than an implementation choice.
key_works: Asharov, Beimel, Makriyannis, and Omri, 2024, *Complete Characterization of Fairness in Secure Two-Party Computation of Boolean Functions*, DOI 10.1137/18M1232656.

title: General NP SNARGs from plain LWE
subfield: Zero knowledge, succinct arguments, and recursive proofs
open: Can we construct succinct noninteractive arguments (SNARGs) for all of NP assuming only plain LWE, with a precise and standard specification of soundness, setup, and succinctness — and without relying on any additional strong commitment assumption?
status: SNARGs for P from LWE are known (Choudhuri, Jain, and Jin, 2021–2022, *SNARGs for P from LWE*), and recent work under stronger assumptions (Guan and Yogev, 2025–2026, ePrint 2025/2328) gives constructions, but none of these settles the target of general-NP SNARGs from plain LWE.
solved_when: A SNARG for general NP is constructed and proved sound under plain LWE alone, with the soundness notion, setup model, and succinctness parameters explicitly specified, and no extra commitment-type assumption beyond LWE.
why: It would give a major new foundation for general succinct verification, replacing stronger-assumption-based SNARGs with the most standard lattice assumption.
key_works: Choudhuri, Jain, and Jin, 2021–2022, *SNARGs for P from LWE*; Guan and Yogev, 2025–2026, ePrint 2025/2328.

subfield: Zero knowledge, succinct arguments, and recursive proofs
open: Can the Micali-based SNARG framework of Guan and Yogev be made sound against adversaries who choose the statement adaptively, after seeing the public parameters, while keeping its current assumption profile and succinctness? Formally, this asks to lift the established nonadaptive soundness to adaptive soundness for statement selection.
status: The current framework (Guan and Yogev, 2025–2026, *Micali's SNARG, Function Vector Commitments, and Fiat–Shamir*, ePrint 2025/2328) explicitly establishes nonadaptive soundness only.

why: Real applications commonly choose statements after seeing public parameters, so nonadaptive soundness alone leaves the framework unusable in the settings it is intended for.

title: Post-quantum recursion matching pairing-based practicality
subfield: Zero knowledge, succinct arguments, and recursive proofs
open: Can a recursive proof system built only on post-quantum assumptions match the practical profile of a leading pairing-based recursive system at comparable security? Concretely, this means simultaneously matching its proof size, verification latency, and prover cost.
status: Post-quantum transparent proof systems exist (e.g., Ben-Sasson et al., 2018, ePrint 2018/046; Kothapalli, Setty, and Tzialla, 2021–2022, *Nova*, ePrint 2021/370), but achieving simultaneous practical parity with pairing-based recursion remains an open, stronger target.
solved_when: A post-quantum recursive proof system achieves, at a comparable security level, the same proof size, verification latency, and prover cost as the pinned pairing-based recursive system.
why: Recursion is the engine of scalable proof-carrying computation; without post-quantum parity, systems that depend on recursive composition have no migration path once quantum adversaries become practical.
key_works: Ben-Sasson et al., 2018, ePrint 2018/046; Kothapalli, Setty, and Tzialla, 2021–2022, *Nova*, ePrint 2021/370.

title: Tenfold smaller transparent proofs without hidden regressions
subfield: Zero knowledge, succinct arguments, and recursive proofs
open: Can transparent proof systems achieve an order-of-magnitude reduction in proof size against a fixed baseline, without paying for it elsewhere? Formally, reduce transparent proof bytes tenfold while holding security level, prover memory, verification cost, and trusted-setup requirements constant.
status: This is posed as a multiobjective moonshot target, not a claim that progress on transparent proof sizes has stalled. The context is the transparent, post-quantum setup line of work exemplified by Ben-Sasson et al., 2018, *Scalable, Transparent, and Post-Quantum Secure Computational Integrity*, ePrint 2018/046; related directions include locally testable codes and proof-length lower bounds.
solved_when: A transparent proof system achieves a tenfold reduction in proof bytes relative to the fixed baseline, with security, prover memory, verification cost, and trusted-setup requirements all unchanged from that baseline.
why: Network and storage costs often determine whether succinct proofs are usable in practice; a size cut that silently inflates verification or prover resources would not deliver that benefit.

title: Restart-safe recursive proof pipelines
subfield: Zero knowledge, succinct arguments, and recursive proofs
open: Can a recursive proof pipeline be made robust to machine-level realities — retries, parallel workers, checkpoints, and restored prover state — without losing the guarantees that make the proofs meaningful? Formally, how do we preserve transcript binding, witness integrity, and a unique ordering of proof steps across such interruptions and concurrent executions?
status: Proposed systems (e.g., Nova, HyperNova) target guarantees beyond the algebraic soundness of an individual folding scheme, but the problem of preserving binding, integrity, and ordering across retries, parallelism, and restored state remains open.
solved_when: A concrete pipeline design and implementation exists in which, under arbitrary restarts, checkpoint/restore cycles, and parallel workers, transcript binding, witness integrity, and unique step ordering are all maintained and verifiable — even though each individual folding step is only algebraically sound.
why: A correct proof primitive can still be embedded in an unsound computation pipeline; without restart safety, a perfectly sound folding scheme yields no end-to-end guarantee about the computation actually proven.

why: It would guide protocol design before an insecure Fiat–Shamir transformation is deployed.

title: Verified compilation from program semantics to proof relations
subfield: Zero knowledge, succinct arguments, and recursive proofs
open: Does the arithmetic circuit that a production zero-knowledge compiler emits faithfully encode the semantics of the source program it was compiled from? Formally, prove that the constraint relation exactly captures the source language's semantics, including arithmetic overflow, memory behavior, exceptional behavior, and nondeterministic inputs.
status: This is a proposed end-to-end target with no existing solution recorded; the soundness of PLONK (Gabizon, Williamson, and Ciobotaru, 2019, ePrint 2019/953) or another backend such as HyperNova (Kothapalli–Setty, 2023) does not establish correctness of the relation supplied to it.

why: An underconstrained circuit can prove the wrong statement perfectly — backend proof-system soundness says nothing about whether the circuit states what was intended.

title: Dynamic stateless-client PIR with near-polylogarithmic work
subfield: Private retrieval, oblivious memory, and encrypted databases
open: Can a database that changes over time be queried privately by many independently initialized clients, each keeping only very small state, while the server's online work per query stays near-polylogarithmic? The question asks for this with update and preprocessing costs counted explicitly, rather than hidden in setup assumptions.

title: Privacy-preserving maintenance of shared PIR preprocessing

why: Static-query benchmarks do not establish a secure continuously updated service; without a maintenance mechanism that handles updates, the reusable preprocessing that makes PIR efficient cannot be deployed on live, changing databases.

title: Concurrent ORAM without security-destroying recovery shortcuts

open: Can we build an ORAM that stays oblivious when many clients operate on it concurrently and the machine crashes mid-operation? Concretely, the position map, stash, eviction, and recovery mechanisms must leak nothing under adversarial scheduling and crash recovery.
status: Existing proposed systems target analyses beyond single-execution bandwidth, but no implementation is known whose position-map, stash, eviction, and recovery behavior remain oblivious under adversarial scheduling and crashes. The problem sits against the backdrop of the Larsen–Nielsen 2018 lower bound (*Yes, There Is an Oblivious RAM Lower Bound!*, ePrint 2018/423) on ORAM bandwidth overhead.
solved_when: A concurrent ORAM implementation exists in which position-map lookups, stash handling, evictions, and crash-recovery paths are all provably oblivious under adversarially scheduled concurrent access and arbitrary crashes — with no recovery shortcut that distinguishes access patterns.
why: Recovery paths can expose which addresses were accessed even when normal operations are fully oblivious, silently destroying the privacy the ORAM was built to provide; a solution would make oblivious memory safe to deploy in realistic concurrent, fault-prone systems.

title: Dynamic volume hiding with low amortized padding

why: Volume patterns alone can reveal the underlying data even when the ciphertexts themselves are secure, so mitigating leakage-abuse attacks requires padding — and the question is how cheap that padding can be made.

solved_when: A leakage accounting framework exists that handles adaptive query histories, evolving auxiliary knowledge, and combinations of multiple encrypted-data services, and yields an interpretable lifetime disclosure budget rather than only per-operation leakage descriptions.
why: Small repeated disclosures can accumulate into near-complete reconstruction, as demonstrated by leakage-abuse attacks, so per-operation analysis gives no honest picture of long-term exposure.

title: Scalable verification of high-order masked implementations
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: Can we verify high-order masked hardware implementations at realistic scale, with time and memory that remain tractable as the masking order and circuit size grow? The goal is a verification method that handles large masked circuits while faithfully modeling glitch effects and compositional interfaces between modules.
status: Strong progress exists, notably Bloem, Iusupov, Krenn, and Mangard, 2018, *Sharing Independence & Relabeling: Efficient Formal Verification of Higher-Order Masking*, ePrint 2018/1031, but historical examples show verification cost growing sharply with order and circuit size.
solved_when: A verification technique exists that checks masked circuits at higher orders with tractable time and memory on large designs, while accounting for relevant glitches and compositional interfaces.
why: As masking complexity grows, an implementation that cannot be verified becomes its own security risk: unverified masking may leak despite appearing provably secure on paper.
key_works: Bloem, Iusupov, Krenn, and Mangard, 2018, *Sharing Independence & Relabeling: Efficient Formal Verification of Higher-Order Masking*, ePrint 2018/1031.

title: Joint glitch, transition, and coupling leakage models
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: Can we build leakage models that jointly capture glitches, transitions, routing effects, and physical coupling — and validate them experimentally — while still being usable for formal verification rather than hopelessly conservative?
status: Existing formal models capture important subsets of the physical behavior, but none achieves experimentally validated joint soundness across glitches, transitions, routing, and coupling; joint soundness remains a stronger target than the current state of the art. Key works: Bloem et al., 2018, ePrint 2018/1031; Barthe et al., 2016, *Strong Non-Interference and Type-Directed Higher-Order Masking*.
solved_when: A compositional leakage model covering glitches, transitions, routing effects, and physical coupling is experimentally validated and supports sound, usable formal verification (i.e., joint soundness without unusable conservatism).
why: A masking proof carried out in an incomplete leakage model can certify security while real physical leakage still escapes detection.
key_works: Bloem et al., 2018, ePrint 2018/1031; Barthe et al., 2016, *Strong Non-Interference and Type-Directed Higher-Order Masking*.

title: Masking-preserving compilation and layout
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: Can a compiler preserve high-order masking guarantees while still performing ordinary backend work — scheduling, register allocation, and instruction selection — together with hardware placement? Formally: is there a verified compilation and layout pipeline whose source-level masking proof is carried through to the emitted code and chip layout?
status: Component-level masking proofs exist, but they do not automatically survive compiler scheduling, register allocation, instruction selection, or hardware placement; relabeling-based techniques (Bloem et al., 2018, *Sharing Independence & Relabeling*) and the HACL*/Vale/EverCrypt line of verified-crypto engineering represent the current toolkit, and verified optimization and physical-design constraints remain open directions.
solved_when: A compilation and layout pipeline is demonstrated (ideally with machine-checked proofs) in which code passing a high-order masking proof at the component level provably retains that guarantee after scheduling, register allocation, instruction selection, and hardware placement.
why: Backend optimization can silently reconnect shares that were separated in the design, so component-level masking proofs established today do not automatically survive these transformations.
key_works: Bloem et al., 2018, *Sharing Independence & Relabeling*; HACL*/Vale/EverCrypt project documentation.

title: Low-overhead higher-order masking of post-quantum signing
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: Can a post-quantum signature scheme be implemented with third-order masking at a genuinely low energy overhead, and can its leakage resistance be validated independently across multiple physical devices?
status: A proposed moonshot. First- and higher-order masking work exists for candidate schemes — e.g., NIST 2025, *mUOV: Masking the Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar Digital Signature Scheme at First- and Higher-Order* — but performance and assurance have not yet been evaluated jointly.
solved_when: A third-order-masked post-quantum signing implementation exists whose energy overhead is declared low against an explicit target, and whose resistance is confirmed by independent leakage evaluations across devices rather than a single-device test.
why: Post-quantum migration must not come at the cost of physical-attack resistance; without masked implementations that are both efficient and independently validated, deployed post-quantum signatures remain exposed to side-channel adversaries.
key_works: NIST, 2025, *mUOV: Masking the Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar Digital Signature Scheme at First- and Higher-Order*; related physical-security presentations.

title: Composable security against combined faults and leakage
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: Can one prove — and demonstrate on real hardware — that a cryptographic implementation remains compositely secure when an attacker wields a declared combination of fault injections and side-channel observations at once, including attacks where faults are used to amplify leakage or vice versa?
status: It is known that separate fault and leakage countermeasures need not compose; no combined composable proof-and-validation framework is established. Related threads include Bauer, 2025, *Fault Attacks against UOV-Based Signatures* and Bloem et al., 2018, ePrint 2018/1031.
solved_when: A proof framework exists that composes fault and leakage countermeasures against a declared combined adversary, together with experimental validation of an implementation against that combination, covering cross-amplification attacks.
why: Separate fault-only and leakage-only countermeasures need not compose, so implementations validated against each threat in isolation may fall to real attackers who combine both physical capabilities.
key_works: Bauer, 2025, *Fault Attacks against UOV-Based Signatures*; Bloem et al., 2018, ePrint 2018/1031.

title: Verified cryptography across foreign-function and serialization boundaries
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: Can a cryptographic implementation's formal proof be extended end-to-end through everything an application actually touches — parsers, foreign-function bindings, memory ownership, encodings, and error handling — so that verified code survives contact with unverified glue? Formally, the goal is a verification methodology (or toolchain) whose guarantees compose across foreign-function and serialization boundaries rather than stopping at the primitive.
status: Verified cryptographic kernels, such as EverCrypt (Protzenko et al., 2020, *EverCrypt: A Fast, Verified, Cross-Platform Cryptographic Provider*), represent substantial progress, but they do not automatically verify every integration layer; the surrounding interoperability and parsing code remains outside the proof. Related work areas include memory-safe interoperability and verified parsing (see also HACL*/Vale/EverCrypt documentation).
solved_when: A verification approach exists that carries correctness and security proofs from a verified cryptographic kernel through the parser, FFI bindings, memory-ownership discipline, serialization encodings, and error-handling paths used by real applications, with no unverified gap at the integration layer.
why: Many exploitable failures occur around rather than inside the mathematical primitive — the glue code is where verified cryptography gets broken in practice.
key_works: Protzenko et al., 2020, *EverCrypt: A Fast, Verified, Cross-Platform Cryptographic Provider*; HACL*/Vale/EverCrypt documentation.

title: Cross-device side-channel generalization benchmarks
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: Can the side-channel community agree on shared benchmark datasets that let us measure whether an attack or defense actually transfers across devices? The target is data spanning different chips, manufacturing variation, aging, temperature ranges, compilers, and measurement setups, with held-out devices reserved strictly for attack evaluation.
status: Currently a proposed data target; existing evaluations train and test on the same device, which does not establish transferable attack or defense performance. Key works include Wang et al., 2022, *Hertzbleed*; Bernstein et al., 2024, *KyberSlash*.
solved_when: Such shared datasets exist, covering the listed axes of variation (chips, manufacturing variation, aging, temperature, compilers, measurement setups), and include held-out devices on which attack performance is evaluated — so that transferable (not same-device) attack and defense performance can be demonstrated.
why: Without it, physical-security claims remain tied to a single laboratory setup; with it, cross-device generalization of attacks and defenses becomes measurable and comparable.
key_works: Wang et al., 2022, *Hertzbleed*; Bernstein et al., 2024, *KyberSlash*.

title: Statistical meaning of “no leakage detected”
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: What does it mean, statistically, when a leakage test reports "nothing detected"? Can we derive useful confidence statements about the amount of leakage present, within explicitly defined adversary and measurement classes, that distinguish mere failure to detect from positive evidence of bounded exploitability?
status: This is currently a proposed methodological target; no such framework exists, and finite experiments cannot in principle certify absence of every conceivable side channel. Related considerations include statistical power and distribution-free testing limits, as highlighted by Wang et al., 2022, *Hertzbleed*, and NIST, 2018, *Recommendation for the Entropy Sources Used for Random Bit Generation*, SP 800-90B.
solved_when: A framework exists that converts a leakage-detection experiment into quantitative confidence bounds on leakage for a stated adversary and measurement class, so that a null result can be correctly reported as bounded rather than absent. (No quantitative targets are given in the record; this is the natural criterion for the problem type.)
why: It prevents negative test results from being overstated as security proofs — a real risk given that finite experiments cannot certify the absence of every conceivable side channel.
key_works: Wang et al., 2022, *Hertzbleed*; NIST, 2018, *Recommendation for the Entropy Sources Used for Random Bit Generation*, SP 800-90B.

title: Optimal randomness consumption for composable masking
subfield: Implementation security, formal verification, and physical leakage
open: How much fresh randomness is truly necessary to mask a circuit at a given security order while keeping the masked gadgets composable? More precisely, determine tight fresh-randomness requirements for specified masking orders and circuit classes, with constructions that retain composability under the declared leakage model.
status: Randomness-efficient gadgets exist (e.g., Bloem et al., 2018, *Sharing Independence & Relabeling*, ePrint 2018/1031; Belaïd et al., 2018, *Tight Private Circuits*, ePrint 2018/439), but global optimality across realistic composition constraints remains unresolved.
solved_when: For the specified masking orders and circuit classes, matching upper and lower bounds on fresh-randomness consumption are established, with constructions that remain composable under the declared leakage model.
why: Fresh randomness can dominate the cost of a masked implementation, so tight bounds directly determine how expensive provably secure masking is in practice.
key_works: Bloem et al., 2018, *Sharing Independence & Relabeling*, ePrint 2018/1031; Belaïd et al., 2018, *Tight Private Circuits* (full title verify), ePrint 2018/439.

bib.title: Optimal randomness consumption for composable masking

title: Optimal bandwidth–healing tradeoffs for post-quantum ratchets
subfield: Messaging, authentication, and key transparency
open: How little bandwidth can a post-quantum ratchet use while still healing from compromise, once messages are asynchronous and lossy and the adversary controls delivery scheduling? Formally, characterize the optimal tradeoff curve between communication cost and healing time in this adversarial setting.
status: Basic post-quantum ratcheting is no longer the unresolved question: Signal's living specification, *The Double Ratchet Algorithm*, includes the Sparse Post-Quantum Ratchet (SPQR) and the Triple Ratchet. The open issue is the optimal tradeoff under asynchronous, lossy delivery and explicit adversarial scheduling, an instance of questions from online communication complexity and intermittent distributed systems.
solved_when: A quantitative characterization of the bandwidth–healing tradeoff exists — ideally matching upper and lower bounds on the communication cost needed to recover post-quantum secrecy after compromise under asynchronous, lossy messaging with adversarial scheduling.
why: A solution tells designers how much traffic a secure messenger must add before it heals from a compromise, letting frequent healing coexist with mobile bandwidth and intermittent connectivity; without it, deployments must guess where to place ratchet updates.
key_works: Signal, living specification, *The Double Ratchet Algorithm*, sections on SPQR and Triple Ratchet.

bib.title: Optimal bandwidth–healing tradeoffs for post-quantum ratchets

title: Multi-device post-quantum post-compromise security
subfield: Messaging, authentication, and key transparency
open: Can a messaging system provide post-compromise security across a fleet of devices when each device may be compromised at a different time? The goal is to handle device linking, unlinking, state synchronization, and stale backups so that security is re-established for all devices after any compromise.
status: The problem is currently a proposed lifecycle target that goes beyond the two-endpoint ratchet model of Signal's *The Double Ratchet Algorithm* and the group-based approach of Barnes et al., 2023, *The Messaging Layer Security Protocol* (RFC 9420). Related directions include distributed revocation and mobile-adversary models.
solved_when: A practical protocol design and implementation exist that maintain post-compromise security across multiple linked devices, correctly processing device linking, unlinking, state synchronization, and stale backups, and going beyond the guarantees of a two-endpoint ratchet.
why: A solution prevents a recovered device from being re-compromised through another device's stale state, which is the natural failure point once messaging security extends beyond two endpoints.
key_works: Signal, *The Double Ratchet Algorithm*; Barnes et al., 2023, *The Messaging Layer Security Protocol*, RFC 9420.

title: Efficient post-quantum group healing with long-offline members
subfield: Messaging, authentication, and key transparency
open: Can a messaging protocol keep authenticated group state with strong post-quantum healing guarantees while tolerating members who stay offline for long stretches — without requiring them to store an unbounded update history or forcing the group to reinitialize?
status: MLS (Barnes et al., 2023, *The Messaging Layer Security Protocol*, RFC 9420) provides a deployed protocol framework, but post-quantum efficiency and offline-state handling remain parameter- and application-dependent open engineering questions.
solved_when: A protocol design exists that maintains post-quantum authenticated group state and healing for members with long offline periods, with update history growth and reinitialization frequency that stay bounded and practical for deployment.
why: Real groups contain intermittently connected devices, so a protocol that cannot accommodate them either leaks stale secrets forward or degrades into unbounded state and repeated rekeying.
key_works: Barnes et al., 2023, *The Messaging Layer Security Protocol*, RFC 9420.
