title: Practical post-quantum deniability with explicit compromise semantics
subfield: Messaging, authentication, and key transparency
open: Can we build post-quantum secure messaging that is efficient enough for practice while offering a deniability guarantee that is precisely defined and provably preserved under the key-exposure and transcript-disclosure scenarios the system is designed to withstand?
status: Authentication, forward secrecy, and deniability are distinct properties, and adding a post-quantum KEM does not automatically establish all three. Relevant context includes Signal's *The Double Ratchet Algorithm* and its post-quantum extensions, along with simulation-based definitions and plausible-deniability models.
solved_when: A post-quantum messaging construction is given, together with a formal deniability definition that explicitly models the intended compromise (key-exposure and transcript-disclosure) scenarios, and a proof that the construction satisfies it while remaining efficient.
why: Users and applications rely on properties stronger than bare confidentiality; without explicit compromise semantics, a post-quantum protocol may silently fail to deliver the deniability its users assume they have.
key_works: Signal, *The Double Ratchet Algorithm* and its post-quantum extensions.

bib.title: Practical post-quantum deniability with explicit compromise semantics

title: Secure backup restoration without resurrecting compromised epochs
subfield: Messaging, authentication, and key transparency
open: What is the weakest freshness guarantee a backup must provide so that restoring encrypted messaging state is safe — that is, restored state cannot reuse old keys or silently undo the post-compromise recovery achieved by ratcheting — and how can such a mechanism be built and deployed?
status: Currently a proposed target with no solution; it is understood that entirely rollbackable local state cannot by itself prove freshness. Relevant background includes Signal's Double Ratchet Algorithm and Barnes et al., RFC 9420, with related work on rollback-resistant storage and secure monotonic state.
solved_when: A characterization of the minimum freshness assumptions required for secure restoration is given, together with a working implementation that restores state without key reuse and without rolling back post-compromise recovery.
why: Recovery and backup features can silently reverse the security gains of ratcheting, letting an attacker resurrect compromised epochs; getting this right makes restore-from-backup safe in deployed end-to-end encrypted messaging.
key_works: Signal, *The Double Ratchet Algorithm*; Barnes et al., RFC 9420.

bib.title: Secure backup restoration without resurrecting compromised epochs

title: Low-latency messaging resistant to global traffic analysis
subfield: Messaging, authentication, and key transparency
open: Can low-latency messaging hide communication patterns from a globally observing adversary — and at what cost in latency and bandwidth? Determine and approach the privacy–latency–bandwidth frontier for interactive messaging under a global observer, accounting for realistic user activity and long-term correlation attacks.
status: Systems such as Vuvuzela (van den Hooff, Lazar, Zaharia, and Zeldovich, 2015, *Vuvuzela: Scalable Private Messaging Resistant to Traffic Analysis*, DOI 10.1145/2815400.2815417) demonstrate strong possibilities using cover traffic, but the underlying tradeoff is not eliminated.
solved_when: A characterization of the tradeoff frontier between privacy, latency, and bandwidth for interactive messaging is established, and constructions approach it under realistic user activity models with long-term correlation.
why: Encryption protects message contents but reveals nothing about who talks to whom; without defenses against traffic analysis, communication graphs leak to a global observer even in encrypted systems.
key_works: van den Hooff, Lazar, Zaharia, and Zeldovich, 2015, *Vuvuzela: Scalable Private Messaging Resistant to Traffic Analysis*, DOI 10.1145/2815400.2815417.

title: Private, abuse-resistant contact discovery at global scale
subfield: Messaging, authentication, and key transparency
open: Can a contact-discovery service support very large, frequently updated directories while keeping individual queries private, limiting enumeration by malicious clients, and staying within mobile bandwidth budgets — all without relying on a single trusted privileged enclave?
status: Scalable private contact-discovery protocols exist (Kales, Rechberger, Schneider, Senker, and Weinert, 2019, *Mobile Private Contact Discovery at Scale*, with accompanying implementation); enumeration resistance and operational leakage remain additional requirements beyond current designs.
solved_when: A deployed protocol handles very large, frequently updated contact directories with private queries, enumeration resistance, and operational leakage control, at mobile-scale bandwidth, under no single privileged enclave.
why: Contact discovery can reveal a user's entire social graph before any message is sent, so weaknesses here undermine the privacy that secure messaging is meant to provide.
key_works: Kales, Rechberger, Schneider, Senker, and Weinert, 2019, *Mobile Private Contact Discovery at Scale*; accompanying implementation.

title: Privacy-preserving global password-guess throttling
subfield: Messaging, authentication, and key transparency
open: Can we throttle distributed online password-guessing attempts without a service that globally tracks user identities? A satisfactory design would bound an attacker's guessing rate under explicit, stated assumptions about Sybil resistance, server compromise, and account recovery.
status: Proposed as a systems problem; it is recognized that cryptography alone cannot impose scarcity on unlimited unauthenticated identities, since Sybil accounts evade purely cryptographic throttling. Relevant works include Jarecki et al., 2018, *OPAQUE*, ePrint 2018/163, and Canetti et al., 2012, *Efficient Password Authenticated Key Exchange via Oblivious Transfer*.
solved_when: A system design is specified in which online guessing against a password-protected account is limited to a defined attempt budget, with all assumptions about Sybil resistance, server compromise, and recovery made explicit and the design's security analyzed under those assumptions.
why: Even the strongest password-authenticated key exchange protocols remain vulnerable to unlimited online guessing, so safe online-attempt limits are a missing piece for practical password security.
key_works: Jarecki et al., 2018, *OPAQUE*, ePrint 2018/163; Canetti et al., 2012, *Efficient Password Authenticated Key Exchange via Oblivious Transfer*.

title: Private key transparency with global equivocation detection
subfield: Messaging, authentication, and key transparency
open: Can a key-transparency system detect globally equivocating servers and malicious key changes while keeping key lookups private, requiring minimal client monitoring, and handling large-scale key rotation and account recovery?
status: CONIKS (Melara, Blankstein, Bonneau, Felten, and Freedman, 2015, *CONIKS: Bringing Key Transparency to End Users*, ePrint 2014/1004) supplies a major baseline; its existence does not settle every privacy, recovery, and deployment tradeoff. Related directions include Byzantine transparency logs and private authenticated dictionaries.
solved_when: A deployed-design-level construction achieves equivocation detection across all clients, lookup privacy, low client monitoring overhead, and scalable key rotation and account recovery.
why: End-to-end encryption fails if users are silently given attacker-controlled keys.
key_works: Melara, Blankstein, Bonneau, Felten, and Freedman, 2015, *CONIKS: Bringing Key Transparency to End Users*, ePrint 2014/1004.

title: Auditable threshold issuance without holder deanonymization
subfield: Anonymous credentials, coercion resistance, and private accountability
open: Can a threshold credential issuance scheme make distributed issuers accountable for unauthorized or inconsistent issuance, while guaranteeing that the audit evidence itself neither identifies honest holders nor links their presentations?
status: Threshold issuance schemes already exist; public accountability of the issuing authorities under malicious behavior has been proposed as a distinct requirement, as in Sonnino et al., 2018–2019, *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344, but it is not realized there together with holder deanonymization resistance.
solved_when: A construction is given in which issuance is threshold-distributed, any unauthorized or inconsistent issuance by authorities produces auditable evidence of malicious behavior, and that evidence provably does not deanonymize honest holders or link their credential presentations.
why: It removes the current forced choice between holder privacy and issuer accountability — privacy should not require unaccountable credential authorities.
key_works: Sonnino et al., 2018–2019, *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344.

bib.title: Auditable threshold issuance without holder deanonymization

title: Minimal assumptions for privacy-preserving credential nontransferability
subfield: Anonymous credentials, coercion resistance, and private accountability
open: Which nontransferability guarantees for privacy-preserving credentials remain achievable when the credential holder willingly cooperates with a buyer, and which hardware, interaction, or external assumptions are provably indispensable to achieve them?
status: Proposed as a classification problem; no such characterization is known. Ordinary software secrets can be copied, so unconditional nontransferability is not presumed. Related areas include copy protection (e.g., Aaronson, 2009, *Quantum Copy-Protection and Quantum Money*) and mechanism design with transferable secrets; Coconut (Sonnino et al.) is a relevant credential scheme.
solved_when: A characterization exists that, for each nontransferability guarantee, either constructs it under explicitly stated assumptions or proves it unattainable without them, thereby identifying the minimal assumptions required.
why: It would cleanly separate genuinely attainable holder binding from misleading security claims, telling credential systems designers exactly what must be assumed to deliver nontransferability at all.
key_works: Sonnino et al., *Coconut*; Aaronson, 2009, *Quantum Copy-Protection and Quantum Money*.

bib.title: Minimal assumptions for privacy-preserving credential nontransferability

title: Anonymous rate limits without universal tracking identifiers
subfield: Anonymous credentials, coercion resistance, and private accountability
open: Can a federation enforce per-holder usage limits while keeping issuers and verifiers unable to reconstruct any holder's cross-service behavior? Formally, the goal is a construction combining anonymous credentials with enforceable per-holder rate limits, such that no collusion of issuers and verifiers can link activity across services.
status: A proposed target exists with explicit enrollment and Sybil assumptions, but anonymity alone does not solve the unique-human enrollment problem. Related efforts include Sonnino et al., *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344, and Kales et al., 2019, *Mobile Private Contact Discovery at Scale*; related areas are Sybil-resistant systems and privacy-preserving quotas.
solved_when: A construction exists that enforces per-holder limits across the federation under its stated enrollment and Sybil assumptions, while preventing issuers and verifiers from reconstructing cross-service behavior of any holder.
why: Many otherwise useful anonymous services collapse under abuse; without enforceable limits, anonymous systems must choose between resisting abuse and preserving privacy.
key_works: Sonnino et al., *Coconut*, arXiv:1802.07344; Kales et al., 2019, *Mobile Private Contact Discovery at Scale*.

title: Tight assumptions for remote coercion resistance
subfield: Anonymous credentials, coercion resistance, and private accountability
open: What is the minimal set of assumptions — private channels, honest devices, or moments of unobserved voter interaction — under which remote voting can resist coercion, given an explicitly modeled coercer? A characterization would delimit, for each declared coercer capability, the weakest assumptions that still suffice.
status: Coercion-resistant protocols exist under assumptions, and complete surveillance cannot simply be wished away; the exact dividing line remains uncharacterized. Foundational work includes Juels, Catalano, and Jakobsson, 2005, *Coercion-Resistant Electronic Elections*, ePrint 2002/165; DOI 10.1145/1102199.1102213.
solved_when: A precise characterization is given of which combinations of private-channel, honest-device, and unobserved-interaction assumptions are sufficient for coercion resistance against a coercer with explicitly stated capabilities, together with a matching impossibility when the assumptions are weakened.
why: It would make election-security claims precise about their unavoidable trust requirements, separating what protocols genuinely achieve from what they silently assume.
key_works: Juels, Catalano, and Jakobsson, 2005, *Coercion-Resistant Electronic Elections*, ePrint 2002/165; DOI 10.1145/1102199.1102213.

title: Large-scale coercion-resistant revoting with practical tallying
subfield: Anonymous credentials, coercion resistance, and private accountability
open: Can coercion-resistant revoting be made to work at realistic national-election scale — say, a declared ten-million-ballot workload — while keeping tallying publicly verifiable, memory bounded, and robust against maliciously crafted submissions?
status: This is a proposed scaling target. Deniable revoting constructions exist (Achenbach et al., 2015, *Improved Coercion-Resistant Electronic Elections through Deniable Re-Voting*), but their benchmark assumptions and tally costs remain the obstacles to scaling.
solved_when: A construction demonstrates coercion-resistant revoting on a ten-million-ballot workload with publicly verifiable tallying, bounded memory, and robust handling of malicious submissions.
why: Without it, strong anti-coercion guarantees remain laboratory results that break down at the scale of real elections; a solution would make deniable revoting deployable in practice.
key_works: Achenbach et al., 2015, *Improved Coercion-Resistant Electronic Elections through Deniable Re-Voting*.

bib.title: Large-scale coercion-resistant revoting with practical tallying

title: Human-verifiable coercion resistance under realistic error
subfield: Anonymous credentials, coercion resistance, and private accountability
open: Can ordinary users actually carry out the security-critical steps of a coercion-resistant protocol under realistic conditions — making mistakes, having accessibility needs, and facing deceptive instructions? The goal is an experimental demonstration of usable, human-verifiable coercion resistance rather than another formal protocol proof.
status: Currently a proposed experimental target; no such study exists, and a formal protocol proof does not establish usable human behavior. Background protocols include Juels–Catalano–Jakobsson, 2005, *Coercion-Resistant Electronic Elections*, and Achenbach et al., 2015, *Deniable Re-Voting*.
solved_when: A user study demonstrates that ordinary users can complete the security-critical steps of a coercion-resistant protocol despite mistakes, accessibility needs, and deceptive instructions.
why: Coercion resistance that depends on reliably performed human actions is only as strong as the humans executing it; without direct evidence that users can perform these steps, the security guarantee may not hold in practice.
key_works: Juels–Catalano–Jakobsson, 2005, *Coercion-Resistant Electronic Elections*; Achenbach et al., 2015, *Deniable Re-Voting*.

bib.title: Human-verifiable coercion resistance under realistic error

title: Practical post-quantum coercion-resistant election proofs
subfield: Anonymous credentials, coercion resistance, and private accountability
open: Can we build an end-to-end verifiable election protocol that is coercion-resistant and post-quantum secure, yet efficient enough for real-world deployment, and whose ballot and audit records remain protected for decades? Formally, the goal is to combine post-quantum ballot privacy, coercion resistance, and universally verifiable tallying with practical proof sizes and explicit long-term archival guarantees.
status: Currently only a joint target has been proposed; existing partial work does not establish the whole election protocol's security — in particular, substituting a KEM or signature into classical constructions does not suffice. Related lines include long-term verifiability and post-quantum proof systems, with foundations in Juels et al., 2005, *Coercion-Resistant Electronic Elections*, and Ben-Sasson et al., 2018, ePrint 2018/046.
solved_when: A single election protocol is constructed that simultaneously achieves post-quantum ballot privacy, coercion resistance, and universally verifiable tallying, with practical proof sizes and explicit long-term archival guarantees, established at the level of the whole protocol rather than by substituting a post-quantum KEM or signature primitive.
why: Ballot secrecy and audit records can need protection for decades, so a quantum adversary emerging even long after election day must not retroactively break voter privacy; a solution makes verifiable elections deployable in a post-quantum world.
key_works: Juels et al., 2005, *Coercion-Resistant Electronic Elections*; Ben-Sasson et al., 2018, ePrint 2018/046.

bib.title: Practical post-quantum coercion-resistant election proofs

title: Complete-liability proofs without a trusted completeness oracle
subfield: Anonymous credentials, coercion resistance, and private accountability
open: What external evidence, if any, must a private solvency proof rely on to establish that all of an exchange's liabilities were included — rather than merely verifying arithmetic over the subset the exchange chose to disclose? A formal characterization would delimit which completeness oracles, if any, are unavoidable.
status: Proofs of assets and committed liabilities exist, as in Dagher, Bünz, Bonneau, Clark, and Boneh, 2015, *Provisions: Privacy-Preserving Proofs of Solvency for Bitcoin Exchanges*, ePrint 2015/1008; however, cryptography cannot automatically discover undisclosed obligations, so current proofs verify only arithmetic over disclosed commitments.
solved_when: There is a precise characterization — an impossibility result showing no private solvency proof can establish liability completeness without some trusted external source, or a construction achieving completeness from specified external evidence — of the evidence needed for a solvency proof to guarantee that all liabilities are included.
why: It would draw the boundary between what cryptographic verification can establish and what depends on real-world accounting truth, determining whether solvency proofs can ever be self-contained.
key_works: Dagher, Bünz, Bonneau, Clark, and Boneh, 2015, *Provisions: Privacy-Preserving Proofs of Solvency for Bitcoin Exchanges*, ePrint 2015/1008.

title: Activation and compositional structure of bound information
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: When does secret correlation that cannot be distilled into a secret key become useful once combined with other correlations? In particular, is there a sharp criterion for when such activation occurs?
status: The 2026 existence theorem (Pauwels, Gisin, and Renner, 2026, *Bipartite Bound Information Exists*, arXiv:2607.25838; building on Maurer–Wolf, 1999) opens a concrete bipartite setting for questions beyond existence.
solved_when: A characterization (with sharp activation criteria, if such exist) is given of when nondistillable secret correlations become useful under composition with other correlations.
why: It determines whether apparently unusable secrecy can serve as a composable resource rather than being inert.
key_works: Pauwels, Gisin, and Renner, 2026, *Bipartite Bound Information Exists*, arXiv:2607.25838; Maurer–Wolf, 1999.

title: Online entropy certification under drift
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Can we certify a conservative lower bound on the usable entropy rate of a physical noise source whose behavior drifts with age or environment, without assuming the stationarity that current testing cannot justify? Formally, this asks for an online certification procedure whose guarantees survive nonstationary noise.
status: Standards (NIST SP 800-90B, 2018, *Recommendation for the Entropy Sources Used for Random Bit Generation*) provide assessment procedures for entropy sources; robust certification under nonstationarity remains a stronger, currently unmet target. Related machinery includes nonstationary statistics and online change detection.
solved_when: A certification method exists that outputs a conservative usable entropy rate valid under drifting, aging, or environmentally changing noise, with no unjustified stationarity assumptions.
why: Randomness failures can invalidate otherwise correct cryptography, so a source whose certified entropy silently degrades under drift undermines every construction built on it.
key_works: NIST, 2018, *Recommendation for the Entropy Sources Used for Random Bit Generation*, SP 800-90B.

bib.title: Online entropy certification under drift

title: Entropy combiners robust to correlated source failures
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: How much nearly uniform randomness can we extract when some of several physical entropy sources may fail or become correlated with each other, and what independence or conditional-entropy assumptions are actually necessary to make extraction possible?
status: A classification and implementation target has been proposed, but combining two weak sources does not automatically produce strong randomness. Key works: NIST, 2018, SP 800-90B; Dodis et al., 2008, *Fuzzy Extractors*, arXiv:cs/0602007.
solved_when: Extraction guarantees are determined for the setting of several sources with possible failures or correlations, with the precise independence or conditional-entropy assumptions under which they hold stated exactly.
why: Redundant randomness hardware is useful only under defensible failure assumptions; without such guarantees, combining sources provides no assurance of strong randomness.
key_works: NIST, 2018, SP 800-90B; Dodis et al., 2008, *Fuzzy Extractors*, arXiv:cs/0602007.

title: Reusable fuzzy extraction under correlated enrollment
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Can noisy biometric or physical measurements be reused across multiple services and enrollments while preserving security? Formally, is there a fuzzy extraction scheme secure when enrollment instances are correlated and realistic auxiliary information is available to the adversary, such that cumulative helper-data leakage stays within a precisely bounded budget?
status: Fuzzy extraction is established in general (Dodis, Ostrovsky, Reyzin, and Smith, 2008, *Fuzzy Extractors: How to Generate Strong Keys from Biometrics and Other Noisy Data*, DOI 10.1137/060651380), but correlated reuse and realistic auxiliary information remain open additional requirements.
solved_when: A reusable fuzzy extractor is constructed (or shown impossible) that supports correlated enrollment and realistic auxiliary information, with the cumulative helper-data leakage across reuses provably bounded by an explicitly stated budget.
why: A biometric cannot simply be replaced after every disclosure, so unbounded helper-data leakage across reuse permanently compromises the underlying secret.
key_works: Dodis, Ostrovsky, Reyzin, and Smith, 2008, *Fuzzy Extractors: How to Generate Strong Keys from Biometrics and Other Noisy Data*, DOI 10.1137/060651380.

title: Optimal fuzzy extraction for edit-like metrics
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Can we build fuzzy extractors that remain secure and correct when secrets are corrupted by insertions, deletions, and misalignment rather than Hamming errors, and that achieve near-optimal entropy loss with an efficient reconstruction procedure — even against adversarial manipulation of the helper data?
status: General frameworks and constructions exist, following Dodis et al., 2008, *Fuzzy Extractors*, arXiv:cs/0602007, but optimality depends strongly on the error metric and robustness requirements; related tools include insertion–deletion codes and document exchange.
solved_when: A construction is given for edit-like (insertion/deletion/alignment) error models that simultaneously achieves near-optimal entropy loss, efficient reconstruction, and robustness to adversarial helper-data manipulation.
why: Hamming-distance models do not capture every noisy physical or biometric source; edit-like errors are the natural model for many such sources, and without suitable extractors their secrets cannot be reliably and securely recovered.
key_works: Dodis et al., 2008, *Fuzzy Extractors*, arXiv:cs/0602007.

title: Realistic conditional biometric-entropy datasets
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Can we build consented, representative datasets that allow conservative estimates of the entropy actually extractable from biometric measurements, conditioned on population information, related measurements, and previously released helper data?
status: Currently a proposed data target only. It is recognized that nominal sensor resolution is not a measure of extractable secret entropy.
solved_when: Such datasets exist and support conservative conditional biometric-entropy estimates that account for population information, related measurements, and prior helper-data releases, without relying on nominal sensor resolution as a proxy for extractable secret entropy.
why: Cryptographic biometric claims require defensible source models; without them, secrecy guarantees for fuzzy extractors and related schemes rest on unvalidated entropy assumptions.
key_works: Dodis et al., 2008, *Fuzzy Extractors*, ePrint 2003/235; NIST SP 800-90B.

title: Steganography under channel-model misspecification
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Can a steganographic encoder retain quantified undetectability when its model of the channel diverges from the distribution an observer actually samples from — and that mismatch itself drifts over time?
status: Provably secure constructions depend on explicit channel or sampling assumptions, and those assumptions need not hold exactly in natural data.
solved_when: A construction (or impossibility result) exists that maintains a quantitative undetectability guarantee under encoder–observer distribution mismatch that changes over time, with the guarantee stated explicitly as a function of the mismatch.
why: Distribution mismatch can overwhelm a theoretically secure embedding method, so provable guarantees that ignore it may fail precisely on natural data.
key_works: Hopper, Langford, and von Ahn, 2002, *Provably Secure Steganography*, ePrint 2002/137; Liao et al., 2025, *A Framework for Designing Provably Secure Steganography*.

title: Robust steganographic capacity under common transformations
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: How much hidden information can be reliably embedded in content that will then be compressed, resized, edited, or re-encoded, without the embedding becoming detectable? Formally, what are the achievable hidden-message rates under a declared family of such transformations while preserving undetectability?
status: Particular robust constructions exist — including Wang et al., 2025, *SparSamp: Efficient Provably Secure Steganography Based on Sparse Sampling*, arXiv:2503.19499, and Qi et al., 2025, on robust-image steganography — but these do not establish a general capacity frontier.
solved_when: A characterization of the achievable hidden-message rates is established for a declared family of compression, resizing, editing, and re-encoding operations, with undetectability preserved throughout.
why: Real communication channels transform content, so hidden messages that cannot survive ordinary processing are unusable in practice; a general capacity frontier would tell designers what rates are actually attainable.
key_works: Wang et al., 2025, *SparSamp: Efficient Provably Secure Steganography Based on Sparse Sampling*, arXiv:2503.19499; Qi et al., 2025, robust-image steganography work.

title: Interactive generative steganography with composable guarantees
subfield: Information-theoretic secrecy, randomness, and tamper resistance
open: Can steganographic communication remain undetectable across a long, adaptive, multi-turn conversation generated on the fly, while keeping latency, sampling cost, and semantic quality practical and recovering gracefully when messages are lost?
status: Proposed systems target; single-message distribution preservation is not a complete interactive security argument. Key works: Ding et al., 2023, *Discop: Provably Secure Steganography in Practice Based on "Distribution Copies"*; Wang et al., 2025, *SparSamp*.
solved_when: A construction exists that provably preserves undetectability over adaptive interactive channels, with explicit control of latency, sampling cost, semantic quality, and recovery from message loss — going beyond single-message distribution preservation.
why: Interactive generative channels introduce state and feedback absent from static examples, so existing single-message guarantees do not compose into an interactive security argument.
key_works: Ding et al., 2023, *Discop: Provably Secure Steganography in Practice Based on “Distribution Copies”*; Wang et al., 2025, *SparSamp*.

title: Quantum lightning from conservative standard-model assumptions
subfield: Quantum cryptography and unclonable information
open: Can quantum lightning — quantum states with publicly verifiable uniqueness — be constructed from standard, independently credible post-quantum assumptions? Formally, is there a construction whose security does not rely on an idealized (generic) model or a fragile special-purpose assumption?
status: Candidate and generic-model approaches exist; note that quantum money and lightning have different security requirements. Key works: Zhandry, 2017–2019, *Quantum Lightning Never Strikes the Same State Twice*, arXiv:1711.02276; Zhandry, 2023–2025, *Quantum Money from Abelian Group Actions*, arXiv:2307.12120.
solved_when: A construction of quantum lightning with publicly verifiable uniqueness is given, with a reduction from a conservative, standard-model post-quantum assumption, and no reliance on idealized models or special-purpose assumptions.
why: Lightning would yield uniquely identifiable quantum objects without any centralized issuance, separating it from quantum money schemes that depend on a trusted bank.
key_works: Zhandry, 2017–2019, *Quantum Lightning Never Strikes the Same State Twice*, arXiv:1711.02276; Zhandry, 2023–2025, *Quantum Money from Abelian Group Actions*, arXiv:2307.12120.

title: Reusable quantum-token experiments with meaningful security evidence
subfield: Quantum cryptography and unclonable information
open: Can a laboratory experiment store and verify the same quantum token repeatedly while producing quantitative evidence of security against counterfeiting, rather than merely observing no-cloning-related behavior? Concretely, the target is a reusable token demonstration with measured rates of honest rejection and degradation under repeated verification, situated in a defensible security model against counterfeiting.
status: This is currently a proposed experimental target. No demonstration exists; observing no-cloning-related behavior alone is not a cryptographic security demonstration. Related capabilities include quantum memory lifetime and fault-tolerant state verification, with theoretical foundations from Aaronson and Christiano, 2012, *Quantum Money from Hidden Subspaces*, arXiv:1203.4740, and Zhandry's *Quantum Lightning*.
solved_when: An experiment demonstrates repeated verification and storage of a quantum token, with quantified honest rejection and degradation across rounds, and an analysis of the security model against counterfeiting.
why: Practical token systems need both durability under reuse and a defensible adversary model; without these, a no-cloning observation alone does not constitute a cryptographic security demonstration.
key_works: Aaronson and Christiano, 2012, *Quantum Money from Hidden Subspaces*, arXiv:1203.4740; Zhandry, *Quantum Lightning*.

title: Characterizing quantum-copy-protectable function classes
subfield: Quantum cryptography and unclonable information
open: Which function families admit efficient quantum copy-protection? Beyond the known obstruction that efficiently learnable functions cannot be protected, we lack useful conditions characterizing what can be copy-protected; the goal is necessary and sufficient conditions delimiting the copy-protectable class.
status: Positive results cover important restricted classes, but the unrestricted classification remains open; Aaronson's 2009 work *Quantum Copy-Protection and Quantum Money* founded the area, and Coladangelo, Majenz, and Poremba (2024, DOI 10.22331/q-2024-05-02-1330) advanced it.
solved_when: A characterization — efficiently checkable necessary and sufficient conditions under which a function family admits efficient quantum copy-protection — is given, going beyond the learnability obstruction.
why: It would identify exactly which software functionality can fundamentally benefit from quantum protection, separating what quantum mechanics offers from what is unattainable.
key_works: Aaronson, 2009, *Quantum Copy-Protection and Quantum Money*; Coladangelo, Majenz, and Poremba, 2024, DOI 10.22331/q-2024-05-02-1330.

bib.title: Characterizing quantum-copy-protectable function classes

title: Broad copy protection without indistinguishability obfuscation
subfield: Quantum cryptography and unclonable information
open: Can we copy-protect broad classes of functions — such as suitable puncturable cryptographic functions — under plain LWE or similarly conservative assumptions, without assuming quantum-secure indistinguishability obfuscation?
status: The 2025 revisited framework of Ananth, Behera, Huang, Kitagawa, and Yamakawa (*Copy-Protection from Unclonable Puncturable Obfuscation, Revisited*, ePrint 2025/1880) obtains strong results from quantum-secure iO plus LWE; removing iO remains the sharper open target.
solved_when: A construction achieving broad copy protection for puncturable cryptographic function classes is proved secure from LWE (or a comparably conservative assumption) alone, with no reliance on iO.
why: It would substantially simplify the foundations of unclonable software, replacing a heavyweight obfuscation assumption with standard lattice-type hardness.
key_works: Ananth, Behera, Huang, Kitagawa, and Yamakawa, 2025, *Copy-Protection from Unclonable Puncturable Obfuscation, Revisited*, ePrint 2025/1880.

title: Useful device-independent key rates under realistic noise
subfield: Quantum cryptography and unclonable information
open: Can device-independent quantum key distribution deliver key rates that real applications can actually use, once realistic imperfections — detection inefficiency, memory noise, drift, and non-independent device behavior — are all accounted for?
status: Only a proposed scaling target exists; current knowledge offers asymptotic positive rates and idealized noise thresholds, which are insufficient. Key experiments include Nadlinger et al., 2022, *Experimental Quantum Key Distribution Certified by Bell's Theorem*, and Anwer et al., 2026, *Experimental Quantum Randomness Generation and Key Distribution with Entangled Photons*.
solved_when: Sustained finite-key rates sufficient for practical applications are achieved under a noise model that includes detection inefficiency, memory noise, drift, and non-independent device behavior.
why: A secure bit generated extremely slowly may not support practical services; without usable rates, device-independent security remains a laboratory demonstration rather than a deployable technology.
key_works: Nadlinger et al., 2022, *Experimental Quantum Key Distribution Certified by Bell’s Theorem*; Anwer et al., 2026, *Experimental Quantum Randomness Generation and Key Distribution with Entangled Photons*.

title: Safe reuse of device-independent cryptographic hardware
subfield: Quantum cryptography and unclonable information
open: Can device-independent cryptographic hardware be safely reused across sessions even though it retains internal memory — and if so, under what isolation and information-flow assumptions? Formally, the goal is to establish enforceable composable guarantees for reused devices with internal memory, allowing bounded inter-session communication while provably preventing leakage of secrets from past sessions.
status: Device independence does not mean independence from every isolation and information-flow assumption. Experimental device-independent QKD has been demonstrated (Nadlinger et al., 2022, *Experimental Quantum Key Distribution Certified by Bell’s Theorem*), but reuse of devices with internal memory across sessions remains without composable guarantees. Related directions include stateful nonlocal games and quantum information-flow control.
solved_when: A composable security framework is established for reused memory-bearing devices, specifying which inter-session communication is permitted and providing mechanisms that provably prevent leakage of past-session secrets.
why: Devices are normally reused, making cross-session memory behavior security-critical; without such guarantees, device independence alone does not protect against information flow between sessions.
key_works: Nadlinger et al., 2022, *Experimental Quantum Key Distribution Certified by Bell’s Theorem*.

bib.title: Safe reuse of device-independent cryptographic hardware

title: Whole-system QKD security including endpoints
subfield: Quantum cryptography and unclonable information
open: Can a deployed quantum key distribution system be certified secure as a whole, including every non-optical component at its endpoints? Concretely, this asks for a composable security account that covers authentication, random-number generation, classical processing, key storage, control software, and physical leakage alongside the optical protocol itself.
status: This is currently a proposed assurance target rather than an achieved result; existing quantum-channel proofs do not verify every endpoint component. Related efforts include device-independent techniques such as Nadlinger et al., 2022, *Experimental Quantum Key Distribution Certified by Bell's Theorem*, and entropy-source certification standards such as NIST SP 800-90B.
solved_when: A demonstration exists in which a composable security analysis of a full QKD system verifies not only the quantum channel but also the authentication, random-number generation, classical processing, key storage, control software, and physical-leakage behavior of the endpoints.
why: An adversary can compromise keys by attacking endpoint components without ever defeating quantum mechanics, so a quantum-channel proof alone leaves the practical system unverified.
key_works: Nadlinger et al., 2022, *Experimental Quantum Key Distribution Certified by Bell’s Theorem*; NIST SP 800-90B.

title: Certified quantum randomness per joule under drift
subfield: Quantum cryptography and unclonable information
open: Can a quantum randomness source deliver an order of magnitude more certified random bits per joule than a pinned complete-system baseline, while its finite-size security guarantees survive realistic device drift?
status: Currently a proposed moonshot with no demonstrated solution; a key caution is that raw detection rate is not the same as certified extractable randomness, so the target must be met in certified bits, not raw counts.
solved_when: A demonstrated system achieves at least a tenfold improvement in certified random-bit production per joule over the pinned complete-system baseline, with finite-size guarantees maintained under realistic drift.
why: Strong randomness generation would become substantially more economical and portable, moving certified quantum randomness from a laboratory demonstration toward practical deployment.
key_works: Anwer, Mahammedi, Muhammad, Mironowicz, and Bourennane, 2026, *Experimental Quantum Randomness Generation and Key Distribution with Entangled Photons*, DOI 10.1103/x13g-h5xm.

title: Tight fairness–latency–resilience frontiers for transaction ordering
subfield: Decentralized protocols and cryptographic economic systems
open: When must a decentralized protocol sacrifice transaction-ordering fairness, and how much, given a network with known timing behavior and a fixed fraction of Byzantine participants? The goal is a complete characterization of achievable ordering fairness under explicit network timing, Byzantine fraction, and latency requirements, together with matching impossibility results showing the frontier is tight.
status: Aequitas (Kelkar, Zhang, Goldfeder, and Juels, 2020, *Order-Fairness for Byzantine Consensus*, ePrint 2020/269) introduced formal order-fairness constructions and established that fairness is not simply equivalent to consensus consistency and liveness.
solved_when: A set of constructions and impossibility results that meet: for stated network timing assumptions, Byzantine fractions, and latency requirements, the constructions achieve order-fairness while the lower bounds match, so no protocol can do better.
why: Adversarial transaction ordering can extract economic value and cause harm even when the underlying consensus is fully correct, so without tight frontiers protocols have no principled way to set their fairness–latency–resilience tradeoffs.
key_works: Kelkar, Zhang, Goldfeder, and Juels, 2020, *Order-Fairness for Byzantine Consensus*, ePrint 2020/269.

title: Encrypted transaction ordering with robust release
subfield: Decentralized protocols and cryptographic economic systems
open: Can a decentralized transaction-ordering protocol keep transaction contents hidden until the ordering is irrevocably committed, while still guaranteeing that ordered transactions are decryptable and executed even when key holders withhold shares, join and leave, or the network partitions?
status: This is currently a proposed integration target; encrypted submission alone does not solve decryption availability or censorship. Related lines of work include fair exchange and Byzantine atomic broadcast (cf. Kelkar et al., 2020, *Order-Fairness for Byzantine Consensus*; NIST, 2026, *Multi-Party Threshold Cryptography*).
solved_when: A protocol specification and implementation exist that hide transaction contents until order commitment and guarantee either threshold decryption of every ordered transaction or a precisely specified safe fallback under adversary-controlled withholding, churn, and network partitions.
why: Content privacy is useful only if adversaries cannot exploit selective release — without a decryption-availability guarantee, encrypted submission alone leaves the door open to censorship.
key_works: Kelkar et al., 2020, *Order-Fairness for Byzantine Consensus*; NIST, 2026, *Multi-Party Threshold Cryptography*.

title: Ground-truth cryptographic-inventory benchmarks
subfield: Migration, benchmarks, funding, and research infrastructure
open: Can we build representative benchmark environments with complete ground truth for all cryptography hidden in binaries, libraries, protocols, certificates, hardware, and archived data? That is, curated testbeds where every cryptographic instance is known and documented, so that discovery tools can be evaluated against verified reality.
status: Currently a proposed data target aligned with ongoing post-quantum discovery work, including the NIST NCCoE *Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography* discovery and interoperability workstreams. Related efforts include software composition analysis and observability of distributed systems, but scanner output alone cannot establish recall.
solved_when: Benchmark environments exist that are representative of real deployments and come with complete ground-truth inventories of cryptography across binaries, libraries, protocols, certificates, hardware, and archived data.
why: Organizations cannot migrate cryptography they cannot find; without ground truth, scanner output alone cannot establish recall, so the effectiveness of cryptographic discovery tools cannot be measured.
key_works: NIST NCCoE, ongoing *Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography*, discovery and interoperability workstreams.

title: Downgrade-safe hybrid migration under real failures
subfield: Migration, benchmarks, funding, and research infrastructure
open: Can a hybrid cryptographic migration be built that still holds its security guarantees when real-world failures intervene — retries, partially upgraded endpoints, fallback paths, middleboxes, and restored older configurations? In other words, when does combining two algorithms in a protocol remain secure not just on the happy path but across the messy downgrade scenarios of an actual deployment?
status: A deployment target has been proposed, but no such demonstration exists; supporting two algorithms does not automatically yield a secure hybrid protocol. Key works: NIST NCCoE, *Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography*, interoperability workstream and SP 1800-38 drafts.
solved_when: A demonstrated, interoperable hybrid migration preserves its security claims under retries, partial upgrades, fallback, middleboxes, and restored configurations — i.e., no realistic failure sequence silently reverts the system to the weaker security level.
why: Migration failures can silently restore the weaker security level, so without downgrade safety the entire benefit of hybrid deployment is lost precisely when it is most needed.
key_works: NIST NCCoE, *Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography*, interoperability workstream and SP 1800-38 drafts.

title: Long-lived signed archives through repeated algorithm replacement
subfield: Migration, benchmarks, funding, and research infrastructure
open: Can an archive of signed records remain verifiable as its cryptographic algorithms are repeatedly replaced over decades, even through key losses and migrations, without requiring trust in evidence generated only after a compromise occurred?
status: A lifecycle target has been proposed; today, replacing a signature algorithm does not automatically preserve decades-old evidence. Key context: NIST NCCoE, *Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography*; NIST, *Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization*.
solved_when: A lifecycle scheme exists in which provenance of decades-old signed records stays verifiable across multiple algorithm deprecations, key losses, and archival migrations, with no reliance on retroactively created evidence after a compromise.
why: Scientific, governmental, and commercial records may outlive every initial signing algorithm, so archives need a migration path that keeps old evidence trustworthy rather than merely re-signing it under today's assumptions.
key_works: NIST NCCoE, *Migration to Post-Quantum Cryptography*; NIST, *Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization*.

title: Common resource accounting for cryptanalytic estimates
subfield: Migration, benchmarks, funding, and research infrastructure
open: Can the cryptographic community adopt a shared accounting scheme that records the full resource cost of an attack — operations, memory capacity and traffic, parallelism, energy, success probability, and quantum error-correction assumptions — rather than a single "bits of security" figure?
status: This is currently a proposed benchmark target; no such common accounting has been adopted, and "bits of security" remains a metric that can conceal materially different cost models. Related work includes Chen et al., 2020, *On the Concrete Security of LWE with Small Secret*, and Kachigar–Tillich, 2017, *Quantum Information Set Decoding Algorithms*.
solved_when: A published benchmark exists that reports, for each attack-cost estimate, its operation count, memory capacity and traffic, parallelism, energy, success probability, and quantum error-correction assumptions, in a form that makes estimates across cryptographic families directly comparable.
why: A single security-bit number can conceal materially different cost models, so parameter choices and migration decisions currently rest on evidence that is not genuinely comparable across cryptographic families.
key_works: Chen et al., 2020, *On the Concrete Security of LWE with Small Secret*; Kachigar–Tillich, 2017, *Quantum Information Set Decoding Algorithms*.

title: Publishable negative cryptanalysis and independent replication
subfield: Migration, benchmarks, funding, and research infrastructure
open: Can the cryptography community sustain a curated repository documenting unsuccessful cryptanalysis searches — the code, the parameter coverage, the compute budgets, the stopping rules — so that null results become inspectable scientific evidence?
status: This is currently a proposed infrastructure gap, not an existing resource. The motivating observation is that failure to find an attack is useful only when the search and its limitations are inspectable, and related positive-result infrastructure shows the model is feasible: Gohr, 2019, *Improving Attacks on Round-Reduced Speck32/64 Using Deep Learning*, with accompanying code, and Chen et al., 2020, ePrint 2020/539.
solved_when: A maintained repository exists containing unsuccessful attack searches with code, parameter coverage, compute budgets, stopping rules, and independently reproduced positive controls.
why: Without it, failed searches are invisible, so effort is duplicated and confidence in cipher security is systematically mis-calibrated; inspectable nulls would reduce both problems.
key_works: Gohr, 2019, *Improving Attacks on Round-Reduced Speck32/64 Using Deep Learning*, accompanying code; Chen et al., 2020, ePrint 2020/539.

title: Sustainable maintenance funding for critical cryptographic libraries
subfield: Migration, benchmarks, funding, and research infrastructure
open: How can the maintenance of widely depended-on cryptographic libraries be funded so that it remains sustainable over time — covering security maintenance, independent review, incident response, and succession — and which concrete funding mechanisms actually work in practice?
status: This remains a proposed funding research target. General open-source contributor surveys (Nagle, Wheeler, Lifshitz-Assaf, Ham, and Hoffman, 2020, *Report on the 2020 FOSS Contributor Survey*) provide a baseline, but do not prove that every cryptographic project faces the same constraints.
solved_when: Candidate funding mechanisms are identified and empirically tested for their ability to sustain security maintenance, independent review, incident response, and succession for widely depended-on cryptographic libraries.
why: Correct cryptography can become unsafe when its maintenance fails; libraries that entire ecosystems depend on are a single point of failure for security.
key_works: Nagle, Wheeler, Lifshitz-Assaf, Ham, and Hoffman, 2020, *Report on the 2020 FOSS Contributor Survey*.

title: Shared independent physical-security laboratories
subfield: Migration, benchmarks, funding, and research infrastructure
open: Can the field establish sustainably shared, independent laboratories giving researchers access to the equipment, expertise, and reproducible testing needed for fault and side-channel evaluation — and can such access measurably widen evaluation coverage and enable independent replication of results?
status: This is currently a proposed funding target; its success criterion is increased independent assurance rather than merely purchasing equipment. Related work includes Bernstein et al., 2024, *KyberSlash*; Wang et al., 2022, *Hertzbleed*; and Nagle et al., 2020, *FOSS Contributor Survey*.
solved_when: Shared access to physical-security testing infrastructure exists and is sustained, with demonstrable measured effects on evaluation coverage and on independent replication of fault and side-channel findings.
why: Expensive testing infrastructure can limit scrutiny of deployed cryptography, so pooled, independent facilities would broaden who can audit real implementations and make reported vulnerabilities reproducible and verifiable.
key_works: Bernstein et al., 2024, *KyberSlash*; Wang et al., 2022, *Hertzbleed*; Nagle et al., 2020, *FOSS Contributor Survey*.

title: Funding proof maintenance after verification milestones
subfield: Migration, benchmarks, funding, and research infrastructure
open: How should the verification community fund and organize the ongoing maintenance of formal proofs as the software around them — compilers, architectures, APIs, and optimized implementations — keeps changing? Concretely, the goal is to develop and evaluate funding models that keep formally verified artifacts synchronized with that evolution.
status: Currently a proposed funding target; no established funding model exists for this task. Related efforts include Protzenko et al., 2020, *EverCrypt*; MIT, 2022, *High-Assurance Cryptography* project; and Nagle et al., 2020, *FOSS Contributor Survey*, alongside work on long-term formal-methods maintenance and research-software sustainability.
solved_when: A concrete funding model for proof maintenance is developed and evaluated against real evolving verified software (changing compilers, architectures, APIs, and optimized implementations).
why: A one-time verification result is not a permanent maintenance mechanism, so assurance can silently decay while the verified software continues to ship.
key_works: Protzenko et al., 2020, *EverCrypt*; MIT, 2022, *High-Assurance Cryptography* project; Nagle et al., 2020, *FOSS Contributor Survey*.

title: A versioned, evidence-linked cryptographic open-problem registry
subfield: Migration, benchmarks, funding, and research infrastructure
open: Can we build a durable, versioned registry of cryptographic open problems that records not just each problem's statement but also its assumptions, parameter regimes, known equivalences, partial results, refutations, and resolution dates — all backed by human-auditable source links?
status: A proposed data-infrastructure target, not yet built. The 2026 secret-sharing resolution (Nir, 2026, ECCC TR26-146) and the bound-information resolution (Pauwels, Gisin, and Renner, 2026, *Bipartite Bound Information Exists*, arXiv:2607.25838) illustrate why static "open problem" lists become incorrect.
solved_when: A versioned registry exists that captures precise statements, assumptions, parameter regimes, equivalences, partial results, refutations, and resolution dates, with each entry linked to auditable sources.
why: It would make a large cross-linked census searchable, maintainable, and resistant to duplicated or obsolete entries — the failure mode that static "open problem" lists fall into once problems are resolved.
key_works: Nir, 2026, ECCC TR26-146; Pauwels, Gisin, and Renner, 2026, *Bipartite Bound Information Exists*, arXiv:2607.25838.
